For Quincy's Chinese community, the American dream lives on, with caveats
When Ziqiang Yuan moved to the U.S. in 1999, democracy was the last thing on her mind. Political speech was suppressed under socialist rule in her native China, and her aversion to politics stayed with her when she emigrated.
“We have a saying in China, ‘不谈政治.’ That means, ‘don't talk about politics,’ ” Yuan said. “You can get in trouble.”
Yuan, 55, goes by Susan now. She left Wuhan for the U.S. to pursue a post-doc in biomedical research, a field that then offered few opportunities in China while demand here was high. She even landed a scholarship.
But when her landlady brought Yuan to a local municipal meeting, eager to show the young grad student what American democracy looked like, something changed in Yuan. She was impressed that ordinary people were even aware of government gatherings, let alone that they could attend.
“That city council meeting really opened my eyes,” Yuan said. “You can have a chance to speak — directly speak — to those officials.”
Decades later, that first brush with local government would lead Yuan to try her chances at politics, a pathway she couldn’t have imagined had she stayed in China.
Yuan is among 175,000 people of Chinese descent who call Massachusetts home, including one in six Quincy residents. For most of U.S. history, Chinese immigrants have journeyed here in hopes of a better life. Their aspirations have varied decade to decade, and person to person. Indeed, ask people in Quincy about the American dream and the answers are as varied as the food options along Hancock and Beale streets.
Interviews with Chinese immigrants spanning multiple generations suggest the allure of the U.S. is being put to the test, amid a torrent of immigration restrictions under President Trump and the emergence of China as the world’s second-largest economy. But for many, the core draw of America remains strong, whether that’s for greater wealth, liberty or cultural freedoms that are elusive in China.
On a recent weekend in a downtown event space in Quincy, seniors in classical Chinese attire acted out the myth of the immortal moon goddess.
The Mid-Autumn Festival celebration was organized by Frank Poon of the nonprofit Civic Education Alliance. Poon came to the U.S. during a wave of Chinese immigration in the 1980s. Ronald Reagan was president, Beijing relaxed restrictions on its citizens’ ability to leave the country and the British would agree to transfer Hong Kong to Chinese control.
Poon said he knows success in the U.S. is far from guaranteed — and it often takes a lifetime of struggle.
“We’re still aiming at the American dream,” Poon said, and that people like him are “willing to invest all our time, all our effort, to make it come true.”
Looking back, Poon said he’s achieved what brought him to America 43 years ago. For him, that success has been more spiritual than something that can be measured.
“My American dream is, ‘I want to have a better life,’ ” he said. “I do have a better family. I do have opportunity to work with the community, and deep inside, in my heart and soul, I feel good.”
But one attendee of the harvest festival had something to say about a dream deferred.
In 1988, Carol Chu followed her future husband to Boston, with little money and no family here.
“The United States is such a freedom country,” she said. “I wanted to enjoy all the opportunity — get the chance to be free, live free, speak freely.”
Soon after they settled, however, Chu began to realize those things might be out of reach. She became pregnant, and her husband developed a severe gambling addiction. The worst part was when Chu lost custody of her son.
“I [was] so disappointed when I came here, because my American dream totally has not come true,” she said.
Instead of returning to her country, Chu stayed in the U.S. in order to be with her son, even if she could only see him one hour at a time.
"The United States is such a freedom country. I wanted to enjoy all the opportunity — get the chance to be free, live free, speak freely."
Chu recently retired after 37 years working for the Postal Service, and as the years have brought her closer to her son, she said she is finally happy here. Now that her boy is grown, Chu plans to split her time between China and the U.S.
“I think my duty is done,” she said.
Over the decades since these folks emigrated to the U.S., China has roared forward as an economic titan, with hundreds of millions emerging from extreme poverty. For the Chinese youth of today, that adds a new dimension to the decision to leave, whether for the U.S. or anywhere else in the world.
At Quincy’s Wollaston Beach, dozens of Chinese youth spread out on the sand, playing mahjong and practicing the Cantonese language. It was a meetup of the Boston Cantonese Club, and DJ Amanda Lou was spinning pop music under a tent.
The recent Boston University graduate is from Macau, a special administrative region of China ruled by the Portuguese until 1999. She spoke about the American ideal more in terms of culture than economic opportunities or political freedom. For her and many other Chinese graduates, Lou said, the exposure to freedom and different lifestyles is a strong motivation to stay.
“In Boston, I can just wear whatever I want, right? I can wear a tank top, shorts, walk outside — nothing will change," she said. "No one's going to stare at you."
At 23, Lou is ready to make a life in Boston. But remaining in the U.S. has never been a certainty for international students. It depends on factors like finding an employer to sponsor a visa petition. And with the current administration looking to add massive fees for foreign worker visas — and to favor “higher-skilled and higher-paid” applicants — big challenges loom for people like Lou.
“What happens if I don't find an employer who's willing to sponsor me?” she said. “Even if they do, what happens if I get fired or something? Definitely very stressful.”
Lou hopes to open a jazz bar in Boston one day, but if America is out of reach, she’ll have to bring her dreams elsewhere.
This kind of uncertainty is well-known to Vincent Lau, an immigration attorney in Boston. Much of his work involves helping American companies secure work visas. Lau said the traditional legal routes still exist, but they have increasingly narrowed under President Trump.
Among an array of measures to tighten rules on student immigration, Lau said consular officers now hold greater discretion to deny visa petitions, making it more difficult to advise parents on the wisdom of sending their kids to the U.S.
“Applying for the visas at the consulates has become much more challenging for Chinese citizens in general,” Lau said, “especially for students.”
On top of that, the administration is cutting research funding and suing elite universities, which Lau said have long been reliable paths to success in America. The administration has threatened to revoke visas for some Chinese students, and it accused Harvard of collaborating with the Chinese Communist Party.
Lau said the draw to study and live in the U.S. remains strong, but those policies are taking a toll.
“When [universities] are not being backed by the government, when they are being attacked by the government, it's not a quote-unquote, safe place,” Lau said. “It's not a place where people want to go.”
The impetus to immigrate has also changed as Chinese universities rise in global rankings. More Chinese youth are pursuing their studies in China. At the same time, an increasing number of students are returning home after graduating overseas.
But for Boston Cantonese Club organizer Alex Ng, China is no promised land. Ng said the Chinese tech economy suffers from a "race to the bottom" mentality, more driven by the search for rock bottom prices than by innovation. Ng said competition for jobs is fiercer in China than in the U.S., and that's especially hard for college grads.

articles.title_orig: Ahead of US, China meeting, Trump and Xi both face crossroads | Opinion
articles.title_zh: Ahead of US, China meeting, Trump and Xi both face crossroads | Opinion
articles.content_orig:
Ahead of US, China meeting, Trump and Xi both face crossroads | Opinion
The Chinese leader has to deal with a legitimacy crisis at home. The U.S. leader knows that Republicans' success in the midterm elections depend on economic relief for the American people, fast.
A leadership summit between any two countries is always cause for pressure-packed preparations by all relevant agencies, but for the Sept. 24 White House U.S.-China summit between President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping, the stakes have arguably never been higher.
China faces the loss of 18 million factory jobs, rampant income inequality and a 70% increase in rural protests between 2024 and 2025.
The United States faces skyrocketing oil prices, persistent threats of escalation from Iran and China’s alarming trade surplus.
For big "bilaterals" like this one set for Thursday, every Cabinet agency and all senior White House staff scurry to put together an agenda. Here are strategies they'll likely submit to the president as bases for memorandums of understanding, which will come from the meetings if executed well.
Trump, Xi should call for a world conference on AI
Trump and Xi, first and foremost, could agree to participate in and lead a world conference on artificial intelligence, with positive usages and safeguards.
Trump must seek a halt to China’s rampant intellectual property theft, which has enabled Chinese companies to save billions of dollars training their AI on American frontier models.
However, because both countries deeply mistrust the other to fairly navigate AI safety on their own, the leaders must address patent and copyright theft laws, and implement AI guardrails against human harm. Offered in a spirit of friendly competitors, this could benefit both countries and the world.
A joint statement could be significant.
Gain more rare earth metals for the United States
In 2025, Beijing began requiring foreign companies to obtain a special government-approved license to ship certain products containing rare earth metals sourced from China.
To obtain these licenses, companies had to share highly sensitive data, including profiles of end-users.
Companies affiliated with foreign militaries would be largely denied licenses unless Washington maintains some information access (now recognizing U.S. military’s dependence on Chinese rare earth elements) but the United States and China could agree on mutual assistance.
There could be higher tariffs or tighter restrictions on China’s access to semiconductors unless China withdraws its expanded license requirements.
Clarify US-China research collaboration
Recently, millions of dollars of Washington funding for colleges has helped Beijing develop critical military technology through academic research involving organizations affiliated with China’s defense industrial base, according to a House Republican report.
In response, clarify and regulate more strongly research collaboration between American universities and Chinese-military-affiliated organizations.
Negotiate guardrails on tech components that can spy
Mounting evidence reveals that Chinese tech components can secretly transmit information to China.
This is a massive national security risk, particularly due to the U.S. military’s reliance on Chinese batteries. Trump must secure restrictions on components sold to the United States with surveillance capabilities.
Maintain strategic ambiguity on Taiwan
Taiwan remains the strictest red line for China, so any diplomatic negotiation requires strategic ambiguity on Taiwan contingencies. Remain vague about whether the United States would militarily support Taiwan in the case of a Chinese invasion.
Keep the $14 billion pending Taiwan arms sale up for negotiation and leave for later after this summit, depending on Xi’s openness to other demands, and signal support for China while keeping future options open to support Taiwan if necessary.
Pledge to reduce oil prices
Washington wants Beijing to buy American goods. Unfortunately, rising oil prices from the Iran war exacerbated production costs in China, slowing down its economic growth, and driving the Chinese to buy fewer American goods.
Trump could pledge de-escalation attempts with Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz to bring down oil prices. Clarify that China should stop buying Iranian oil until the Strait of Hormuz is opened, and that China should expand its agreement to import more American agricultural goods.
Cooperate on drug policy, target methamphetamine and fentanyl
Expand the McCaffrey-China anti-drug agreement made more than a quarter-century ago on methamphetamine and now fentanyl.
In 2000, retired Army Gen. Barry McCaffrey, as head of the Office of National Drug Control Policy, led a delegation to China and negotiated a drug treatment and source prevention agreement. He explained that for China itself, treatment was more than warehousing thousands of addicts cold turkey in a big room in a Chinese city. It meant stop allowing import of drugs from Myanmar, formerly known as Burma, and providing jobs and counseling for addicts.
Now, China is a major source of devastating fentanyl in the United States. An agreement to help each other could be a productive component of the Trump-Xi summit.
To solidify long-term trust, Trump should increase cultural ties between the two nations by renewing a commitment to sharing arts and sports – like Chinese table tennis and U.S. football diplomacy – and inviting China’s National Peking Opera back to the United States.
Both Trump and Xi are at a crossroads
Xi faces a legitimacy crisis. While many of his citizens have long supported the Chinese Communist Party’s overall economic prosperity, China’s stagnating economy and skyrocketing youth unemployment have greatly weakened the party's internal political legitimacy.
For his part, Trump’s reversing his low approval ratings ahead of the November midterm elections (and, consequently, the Republican Party’s success) depends on his ability to deliver economic relief, and fast. That can be accomplished by increasing American exports to China.
Chinese leaders are as interested in making productive deals with the United States as we are with them, making the Trump-Xi summit an enormous opportunity for the two global superpowers as well as the world.
Robert Weiner was a spokesman in the Clinton and George W. Bush administrations, the White House drug policy spokesman, chief of staff for the House Aging Committee, and communications director of the House Government Operations and Oversight Committee. Emmbrooke Flather is a senior policy analyst at Robert Weiner Associates, and served as copresident of the Chinese Culture Club at Phillips Academy Andover. At Boston College, she studied Mandarin, East Asian Security and the Rise of China.

articles.title_orig: Egypt, China unearth wine press at temple to ancient goddess
articles.title_zh: Egypt, China unearth wine press at temple to ancient goddess
articles.content_orig:
A limestone structure believed to have once served as a wine press was recently unearthed at the Temple of Sekhmet site near the village of Mit Rahina, the Egyptian Tourism and Antiquities Ministry announced earlier this month.
Mit Rahina is located near the ancient ruins of Memphis, which in antiquity had served as the capital of the first nome of Lower Egypt.
In ancient Egyptian mythology, Sekhemet is considered both a warrior goddess and a goddess of medicine. Her temple makes up one part of the Great Temple of Ptah complex, which served as the main temple of ancient Memphis.
Discovered by a joint Egyptian-Chinese archaeological mission, the wine press includes an upper basin sloping downward toward a central opening and a lower collection basin, each topped with an opening designed to hold amphorae.
Archaeologists found grape seeds inside the press, supporting the archaeologists’ interpretation.
Dr. Hisham El-Leithy, Secretary-General of the Supreme Council of Antiquities, explained that the mission began its work by cleaning and documenting the Temple of Sekhmet as part of its excavations to understand how the site was used throughout the ages.
Mudbrick residential complex also unearthed
Additionally, the mission found the remains of a mudbrick residential complex in the area surrounding the temple, along with a series of stone blocks and statue fragments believed to have been part of Ptah’s temple.
Most of the blocks and fragments date back to the New Kingdom period, mainly during the reign of King Ramesses II, and are made from various types of stone, including limestone, red granite, and schist
Other artifacts found at the site include pottery shards, faience amulets, small terracotta and limestone statuettes, ostraca, and votive stelae.
Mohamed Abdel-Badie, head of the Egyptian Antiquities Sector at the Supreme Council of Antiquities, explained that these discoveries indicate that there had been continuous human settlement in the area between the Third Intermediate Period and the Late Period, through the Ptolemaic era and up to the Greco-Roman period.
Egypt’s Tourism and Antiquities Minister Sherif Fathy expressed his pleasure at the collaboration between Egypt and China, two of the oldest civilizations in history.
The Temple of Sekhmet was discovered by chance in 1959, during the construction of a house in the area. Following this, Egyptian antiquities inspector Mohamed Abdel Tawab El-Hetta carried out a single season of excavations at the site from 1961 to 1962.
In 2015, the visible remains of the temple were documented as part of the Ancient Memphis Site and Community Management Project.
Deity-inscribed tombstones, sarcophagi unearthed at ancient Egyptian burial site
Earlier this summer, some 20 limestone tombstones, several sarcophagi, and a collection of funerary amulets were discovered during excavations at the Tell El Deir archaeological site.
The sides and backs of the tombstones are decorated with religious symbols and godly imagery, including that of a griffin, Agathodaemon, and Isis-Thermouthis.
Agathodaemon is a lesser serpent demon in ancient Graeco-Egyptian religion, as well as in classical Greek mythology. Isis-Thermouthis is a combination of the Egyptian goddess Isis, the sister and wife of Osiris, and Renenutet (Thermuthis), the Egyptian goddess of grain.
The appearance of the two deities on the tombstones points to joint Greek and Roman influence on ancient Egyptian heritage and funerary practices.
Further, the decorations allow archaeologists to identify the social status of the tombstones’ owners.
Additionally, the Egyptian archaeological mission operating at the site uncovered a collection of pottery incense burners, decorated lamps, and funerary amulets, as well as several barrel-shaped anthropoid ceramic coffins.

articles.title_orig: Nolan Wells’ family vows to ‘never stop’ seeking the truth after grand jury report
articles.title_zh: Nolan Wells’ family vows to ‘never stop’ seeking the truth after grand jury report
articles.content_orig:
Nolan Wells’ parents and their attorneys called on Mississippi to continue pursuing a fuller picture of the “truth” in the teenager’s death at a news conference Tuesday.
The news conference was held a day after the Jackson County district attorney said a state grand jury will not pursue charges in the teenager’s July Fourth death.
“Jackson County District Attorney Angel Myers McArthur will have you accept that Nolan Wells’ death can be summarized in three words: ‘We’ll never know,’” attorney Ben Crump said. “But Nolan’s family offers three other words: ‘We’ll never stop.’”
Crump, in his remarks, insinuated that the district attorney’s investigation was not exhaustive and should continue until the cause of Wells’ death is made clear.
Wells’ mother, Christine Wells-Wonsley, said she received a text message from the district attorney at 7:54 p.m. Monday, and that the report was released shortly after.
“To me, that action shows a lack of empathy,” she said.
Wells-Wonsley continued: “What we have learned is that we still have no answers, and the report reinforced the fact that Nolan was not given a thorough, transparent and honest investigation.”
The DA’s office shared the text with NBC News. It alerts Wells-Wonsley to the grand jury report, without revealing its conclusions. The DA offers to send it to Wells-Wonsley and offers to “support you in your grief.”
Wells, 18, was last seen celebrating the July 4 holiday with friends on Horn Island, a barrier reef off Mississippi accessible only by boat. The friends he was with that day have said they had to leave the island early because their boat was taking on water, and that Wells opted to stay behind for the rest of the day and told them he’d catch a ride back to the mainland with others.
His body was found at the northwestern tip of the island July 6, Crump has said.
In the aftermath of Wells’ death, Crump pointed the blame toward the friends Wells was with on that day, all of whom are white, and alleged that race played a role. Wells appeared to be one of the few Black people on the island that day, according to photos and videos shared of the celebrations.
District Attorney Angel Myers McIlrath attempted to put that idea to rest with Tuesday’s statement.
In a video message, she said the grand jury did not find sufficient evidence to indict anyone with a crime.
“There is absolutely no evidence to support the allegations that Nolan’s disappearance and death were racially motivated,” Myers McIlrath said. “Nolan’s friends loved Nolan, and Nolan loved them. Nolan chose to stay on the island that day, and there is not a scintilla of evidence to contradict that.”
In an interview with NBC News, Wells-Wonsley said that “at no point in time have we ever made this a racial thing” but that “Unfortunately, the optics of the situation has kind of allowed a segue to that.”
She said that she and her husband, Elmore Wonsley, have only wanted to find out what happened to their son.
“I have always told our children, ‘I will move heaven and earth if anything were to ever happen,’ and that’s exactly what Elmore and I are doing,” she said.
Myers McIlrath took aim at Crump and his team on Monday, saying they’d previously informed her office that they’d found no evidence a crime had been committed against Wells.
Speaking with NBC News on Tuesday, Crump said he did not want to engage in a “tit for tat” with the DA and her office.
“The issue is about what happened to Nolan Wells,” he said. “Everything else is just a distraction.”
The Rev. Al Sharpton, who has been an advocate for the family, said skepticism is warranted from Wells’ parents and those following the case.
“Mississippi’s history painfully teaches us exactly why families should never be expected to simply accept unanswered questions surrounding the death of a young Black person,” the civil rights advocate said in a statement Tuesday.
Crump, along with Wells’ parents, commissioned an independent autopsy, which found the cause of the teenager’s death was “undetermined.” It did, however, find two bruises on the back of Wells’ head.
“To this day, not one person has explained how they got there,” Crump said in a statement. “We don’t know how Nolan died, and neither does the state of Mississippi. Mississippi must keep investigating.”
Crump and Wells-Wonsley both spoke about the apparent blunt force trauma again Tuesday at the news conference and called for answers.
The grand jury’s report, a partially redacted copy of of which was posted to the DA’s Facebook page, noted the bruising to the back of Wells’ head but concluded that it was “not a fatal injury.” A witness, it said, testified to seeing Wells awkwardly off the boat. The witness couldn’t tell if Wells hit his head but said he continued to socialize, the report stated.
Crump also called on the district attorney to release the full autopsy report from the medical examiner’s office.
Coroner Bruce Lynd said he will not be releasing the state’s autopsy report, telling NBC News the report, “which may include a toxicology report, cannot be released because the release of autopsy reports” is limited by Mississippi law.
The grand jury concluded that there was no evidence that Wells had any sort of physical altercation or argument with anyone the day he was last seen. It added “that the position of, the condition of, time of discovery, and location of Mr. Wells’ body is consistent with drowning.”
Crump and Wells’ parents have previously rejected the idea that he simply drowned, citing the teenager’s athleticism and ability to swim. Those who know the area well, though, told NBC News it is not uncommon for even a good swimmer to be swept away by the currents.
The state’s chief medical examiner and a forensic pathologist retained by Wells’ family both “opined that the cause and manner of Mr. Wells’ death is undetermined and that drowning is a diagnosis of exclusion,” according to the grand jury report. It noted, however, that neither has ruled out accidental drowning as a cause.
Crump said there will be another press conference in Orlando, Florida, later this week to discuss the investigation into Wells’ cellphone. The friends on the boat had his phone and brought it back to the mainland from Horn Island on July 4. They said Wells accidentally left it with them, but his parents have refuted that assertion, asking what teenager would leave their phone behind?

articles.content_orig:
Hurricane Polo an extremely powerful Category 4 storm off Mexico's Pacific coast. See its path.
Hurricane Polo, an extremely powerful Category 4 storm, continued to swirl off Mexico's southwestern coast early Wednesday but was only expected to skirt the Pacific shoreline over the next few days, not make landfall, as it continues along its path.
The U.S. National Hurricane Center said Polo's maximum sustained winds — which had rapidly intensified Tuesday, reaching as high as a 180 mph — decreased somewhat to 155 mph, just beneath the 157 mph threshold which would make it a Category 5, the strongest on the hurricane scale.
The storm is expected to fluctuate in intensity over the next few days, forecasters said, but remain a "very powerful major hurricane."
Maps show Hurricane Polo's path
As of early Wednesday, Polo was located about 185 miles off the coast of Zihuatanejo, a coastal resort city in the Mexican state of Guerrero. Polo's outer rain bands were starting to reach the coast, the hurricane center said.
It hurled hurricane-force winds outward up to 40 miles from its center and tropical storm-force winds some 105 miles out, but was roughly stationary, crawling northward at 2 mph.
Polo was forecast to bring tropical storm conditions to parts of the coastline starting Wednesday. In some areas, heavy rainfall "may produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas of steep terrain," the hurricane center warned.
The storm remains far south of Mexico's Baja California peninsula, but the longer-term forecast indicates it could turn in that direction early next week.
The Mexican government issued a tropical storm warning for a stretch of the Mexican coast from Tecpan de Galeana, in Guerrero, to Punta San Telmo, in Michoacán. A tropical storm watch was in effect from Punta San Telmo to Playa Perula, in the state of Jalisco. Tropical storm warnings are issued when forecasts indicate tropical storm conditions will develop in a particular area, while tropical storm watches are issued when those conditions are possible, but not imminent.
In this case, the hurricane center said people under a tropical storm warning should expect those conditions to take shape on Wednesday. For those in the watch area, such conditions could develop by Thursday.
Parts of Guerrero and Michoacán may receive between 3 and 6 inches of rainfall as Polo barrels past, with up to 8 inches possible in certain spots, through Thursday. Between 2 and 4 inches of rain could also fall in coastal parts of the states of Oaxaca, Colima and Jalisco through Thursday, forecasters said.
Along with rain, Polo was also expected to cause life-threatening surf conditions, including rip currents, along the southwestern Mexican coast.
Polo is the second strongest hurricane on record in terms of its central pressure in the Eastern Pacific (behind Patricia in 2015) and tied for third strongest in terms of wind speed (along with Rick in 2009)..

articles.title_orig: U.S. Rebukes Australia Over Proposed Limits on Social Media Algorithms
articles.title_zh: U.S. Rebukes Australia Over Proposed Limits on Social Media Algorithms
articles.content_orig:
US criticises Australia's proposed algorithm opt-out laws as 'censorship'
The US has criticised Australia's proposal to give users the ability to opt out of social media algorithms, saying it amounts to "censorship of protected speech".
Under Australia's draft digital duty of care laws, tech firms risk hefty fines if they fail to give users the option to turn off algorithms in a bid to protect them from harmful content.
In a rare submission to the proposed laws, the US embassy in Canberra said it had "serious concerns" and allowing the government to "enforce vague definitions of 'harm'" would lead to "viewpoint-based censorship".
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the legislation was not about giving governments control but giving it back to individuals.
"We ask that Australia clarify how exactly 'harm' and 'risks' shall be determined... ensuring these definitions do not encroach on protected speech," the US said in its submission.
The US also claimed that the proposed laws may risk "reducing the reach of independent journalists or other voices whose content touches on sensitive or controversial topics" if tech firms had to "pre-emptively demote" them.
An opt-out option would "allow regulators to impose rigid, one-size-fits-all platform design requirements" on tech firms and this could affect users outside of Australia, it said.
"Mandated platform design features, especially when applied to algorithms, may affect what users see, say, and hear not just in or from Australia, but globally."
The US also called on Australia to address industry concerns that the "biases and preferences" of government officials do not "disadvantage independent or minority-viewpoint speech".
Another worry was that the proposed laws could affect Australia's "reputation as a jurisdiction that enables innovation," the submission said.
The criticism comes during Albanese's visit to the US to speak at the UN's General Assembly about his government's tech policies.
On Tuesday, local time in New York, Albanese responded to the criticism and claims of the proposed laws being government overreach.
"It's not about giving government control," he told the media in New York.
"It's about giving people back control over what they receive on their devices."
US President Donald Trump meanwhile used his speech at the UN to play down fears about AI, rejecting proposals for guardrails on it and arguing it should be renamed "super intelligence" as "the use of the word artificial makes it sound fake".
This latest move by Australia to protect its online users from harm comes less than a year after the country introduced a social media ban for children under 16 last December.

articles.title_orig: Soybeans, planes and rare earths: What they say about fragile U.S.-China trade truce
articles.title_zh: Soybeans, planes and rare earths: What they say about fragile U.S.-China trade truce
articles.content_orig:
Soybean purchases, orders for Boeing aircraft and access to rare earths elements — three of the headline commitments underpinning the U.S.-China trade truce — are progressing at markedly different speeds ahead of the summit between U.S. President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping in Washington on Thursday.
Taken together, the uneven fulfillment record suggests the truce is performing its minimal function of keeping commerce moving and discouraging renewed escalation, but there is little willingness on either side to cede strategic leverage, analysts said.
"The truce is moving fastest where it costs least," Eric Xiao, head of sales for Asia at CMC Markets, told CNBC.
The superpowers' May meeting reaffirmed Beijing's commitment to increase purchases of U.S. soybeans and buy 200 Boeing aircraft, while Chinese shipments of rare earths magnets are back underway after export controls were suspended for a 12-month period beginning last November.
But delivery across the three commitments has been uneven, and difficult to verify in some cases.
Larry Hu, head of China economics at Macquarie Group, described the recent U.S.-China relationship as a phase of détente — a cooling of tensions — driven by "a balance of vulnerability."
Both sides are "acutely aware of the other's choke points," Hu said in a note.
The détente should not be mistaken for a rapprochement, according to Wendy Cutler, vice president of the Asia Society Policy Institute.
"Each side has an interest in stability right now," Cutler told CNBC's "The China Connection" in May. "This doesn't mean we're going to become best friends, but it means we're going to coexist."
Soybeans: most visible lever
Soybeans offer the clearest numerical signal of progress across the trade commitments.
China has bought almost half its 25 million ton annual commitment after it purchased roughly one million tons from U.S. producers in a single week in September, Reuters reported.
Soybean purchases are also an important tool for signaling cooperation between the two nations.
"Things pick up a little bit before the bilateral meetings between Trump and Xi ... and then fall off again," China strategist Andy Rothman told CNBC's "Squawk Box Asia" in July, noting that purchases tended to cluster around key meetings.
Xiao described soybean purchases as "political trophies", but cautioned against interpreting soybean fulfillment as a direct sign of Beijing's stance on broader trade ties. "China buys them because it needs them," he said.
Soybean trade tiffs are not a recent development.
China, the world's largest soybean importer, saw U.S. soybeans plummet from 40% of total imports before Trump imposed tariffs on major Chinese goods in 2018, to 23% in the first five months of 2026.
Aircraft: slower, stickier pledge
Progress on the 200-aircraft commitment is less transparent.
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer this week said roughly 140 aircraft were in a "good state," with orders for another 10 being written, according to Reuters. Customers, models and delivery timelines have not been disclosed.
Boeing CEO Kelly Ortberg has also downplayed expectations for a single 200-aircraft announcement, saying individual Chinese airlines would place and announce orders at their own pace.
The pledge came with additional caveats, with Beijing's official account of the May agreement tying the purchases to U.S. guarantees over the supply of aircraft engines and parts.
Rare earths: strategic leverage remains
Beijing's fulfillment of the rare earths commitment is harder to measure, because the promise concerns reliable access rather than a specified export volume.
Chinese shipments of rare earths magnets to the U.S. recovered after earlier restrictions, but fell to 512 metric tons in August — down 20% from July and 13% from a year earlier, according to Chinese customs data reported by the Financial Times.
Uncertainty around rare earths access also persists for U.S. customers.
Some Chinese suppliers have declined U.S. orders because of geopolitical and compliance concerns, while some American companies have waited more than six months for export licenses, Reuters reported.
Rare earths' strategic importance may provide the clearest signal of each nation's stance on trade ties because of the strategic cost of making concessions over the materials, experts said.
Macquarie's Hu identified rare earths as the principal Chinese choke point, balanced against U.S. leverage in advanced semiconductors used in chipmaking.
Xiao similarly called rare earths the clearest indicator of the broader relationship, due to their importance in clean energy, advanced technology and defense.
Progression on the rare earths commitment could "anchor a durable relationship in a way that soybean and aircraft orders cannot," Xiao said.
He noted that exercising that leverage is a delicate calculation. A complete cutoff of exports would encourage the U.S. and its allies to accelerate alternative supply chains while hurting Chinese producers that depend on global electric vehicle and technology markets.
China's "strongest card, in other words, is one it cannot play in full," Xiao said.
– CNBC's Evelyn Cheng and Anniek Bao contributed to this story.

articles.title_orig: Trump-Xi summit puts AI safety talks on the table but neither side wants to slow down
articles.title_zh: Trump-Xi summit puts AI safety talks on the table but neither side wants to slow down
articles.content_orig:
Donald Trump wants the U.S. to beat China in the AI race. But as he meets Chinese President Xi Jinping, both countries are also weighing how to address the risks posed by rapidly advancing technology.
In recent months, AI systems have taken more consequential actions online: OpenAI said one of its research models gained unauthorized access to parts of the AI platform Hugging Face, while Anthropic found AI was being used to automate parts of cyberattacks. The incidents have raised fears that increasingly autonomous models could make attacks faster and harder to contain.
Ahead of Trump and Xi's meeting on Thursday, U.S. Treasury Scott Bessent discussed the prospect of a "U.S.-China AI dialogue" with his Chinese counterpart, He Lifeng, over the weekend, including a channel for incidents "up to a national security level."
"Leaders in both countries are spooked by the increasing cyber capabilities of AI models, and especially agents acting autonomously to escape containment and breach websites," Aalok Mehta, director of the Wadhwani AI Center at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, told CNBC.
But as fears have intensified, tensions have not dissipated.
Washington continues to restrict China's access to Nvidia's most advanced AI chips and has accused Chinese AI companies of using "distillation" — training models on the output of more advanced U.S. systems — a claim Beijing rejects.
While the U.S. took an early lead in developing large language models (LLMs), thanks to companies like OpenAI and Anthropic, Chinese models have made big capability gains in recent months and are increasingly being adopted by companies globally, including in America.
Trump previously dismissed warnings that AI poses an existential threat to humanity, risks amplified by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Anthropic chief Dario Amodei as they called for an industry slowdown and regulatory oversight.
"If we don't win AI, we're going to be put in a very bad position," Trump told reporters earlier this month.
But in a Truth Social post on Monday, he said the government "will rein things in if we have to."
AI safety and access to chips
The likeliest areas of agreement between the U.S. and China could be common definitions and frameworks for AI safety for powerful models and an emergency communication mechanism to discuss incidents, Mehta told CNBC.
A channel for relating national security-related incidents would be a "modest" but positive step, Chris McGuire, senior fellow for China and emerging technologies at the Council on Foreign Relations, told CNBC.
But an agreement to slow down AI's breakneck development speed is "extremely unlikely," he added.
China has historically used AI dialogues "to complain about U.S. export controls," McGuire said, which the U.S. uses to prevent the most advanced AI chips from being sold to China.
"Its state media has largely rejected the concerns expressed by leading U.S. AI labs about the potential for catastrophic risk, which is consistent with China's long-held skepticism of all U.S. arms control proposals," he added.
Despite U.S. restrictions, several Chinese firms have reportedly been able to access the chips' compute power remotely, via data centers in Southeast Asia.
While U.S. trade representative Jamieson Greer said controls on chips were not on the agenda during preliminary talks on the weekend, China could push to have them relaxed, said Melanie Hart, senior director of the think tank Atlantic Council's Global China Hub.
"China's asking the U.S. to embrace Chinese AI models and drop some of the U.S. controls on China's access to semiconductor chips," she told reporters on Tuesday.
Distillation could also come up in the talks. U.S. companies and officials have accused Chinese labs of using the practice to gain ground, characterizing it as theft; China rejects the allegations.
In July, Bessent threatened sanctions against companies doing it and said the Trump administration had found "watermarks of our U.S. large language models on many of the Chinese models," calling it "unacceptable."
Progress on AI cooperation relies on two things, said Mehta. "The first is that it can't hurt the ability for the U.S. and China to compete on the merits of their technology."
The second is a verification mechanism, he added. "Policymakers won't be inclined to take their counterparts just on their word, so we'll need to find ways to ensure information flowing between the two countries is accurate. That means both technical and governance verification tools."

A look at the Chinese leader’s aircraft, which is bound to become part of the visual choreography of his state visit in Washington
The aircraft carrying China’s leader, often referred to in state media and official statements as a zhuan ji, or special plane, remains far less known to the world than Air Force One, despite both countries using Boeing 747s for presidential travel.

articles.title_orig: Trump tells U.N. he could ‘annihilate’ Iran but expects a deal after the midterm elections
articles.title_zh: Trump tells U.N. he could ‘annihilate’ Iran but expects a deal after the midterm elections
articles.content_orig:
In a speech to world leaders at the United Nations General Assembly, President Donald Trump defended the Iran conflict and said he was considering whether to “annihilate” the country and drive it “into hell.”
Or, he said, Iran could make a deal with the U.S. that would allow the nation to rebuild. But that won’t happen until after the midterm elections in November, Trump predicted.
“I believe we’ll make a deal right after the election because it doesn’t make sense for them not to,” Trump said. “They’re waiting to see how I do in the midterm election.”
Trump later said U.S. envoys met with Iranian officials for three hours on the sidelines of the gathering, an unexpected development that offered a glimpse of diplomatic activity.
But Trump has repeatedly floated new attacks on Iran, even previously threatening death to the entire civilization. On Tuesday, he revived that warning at one of the most prominent platforms for world leaders, with an Iranian delegation in the audience.
“I have a big decision to make,” he said. “Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before, maybe one of the greatest in the Middle East or even the world? Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?”
“Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?” he continued.
Most important, Trump said to applause, is ensuring that “Iran will never have a nuclear weapon.”
Iran’s nuclear potential was “the reality we had to confront,” he argued, and “a reality that far too many preferred to ignore.” Tehran has insisted its nuclear program is for civilian purposes and denied having plans to develop nuclear weapons.
The U.N. assembly comes as the Iran war is about to enter its eighth month.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian is scheduled to address the U.N. on Wednesday. Trump told Fox News that he would “probably” be open to meeting with Pezeshkian but did not announce any specifics.
Trump also highlighted peace deals he has worked on, U.S. actions in the Western Hemisphere and progress on his 20-point peace plan in the Gaza Strip.
Trump’s remarks to the assembly this year come as the U.N.’s Human Rights Council found in a report last week “reasonable grounds to believe” that the U.S. had committed war crimes during “indiscriminate attacks” against an Iranian school and a residential area in February.
The American president traditionally addresses the General Assembly each year.
During his wide-ranging speech, the president said America is “doing better than ever before,” touting the U.S. economy and his approach to immigration and artificial intelligence.
Less than a minute into his remarks, Trump called the U.S. economy “the envy of the world” and pointed to his administration’s tax policy and stock market records.
“Our economy is the envy of the world,” he said. “Our military is the most powerful on Earth. Our technology is second to none, and we are leading in virtually everything.”
Many American voters, though, don’t appear to agree. An NBC News poll conducted in September found that 56% of registered voters disapprove of the job the president is doing, and 55% said they believe his policies hurt the economy.
Gas prices remain high, sitting at an average of $4.47 per gallon, about a 50% increase since the war with Iran began. Diesel prices also spiked, affected by the Iran war as well as the war between Russia and Ukraine. Diesel hit a record $6 per gallon earlier this month before surging higher to $6.52 as of Tuesday, according to AAA.
Later, the president touted his record on immigration, tying his crackdown on the southern border to a drop in violent crime in the U.S.
“The entire world is being lifted by the wealth, strength, spirit and momentum of a newly energized and a very powerful United States of America,” he said.
While Trump declined to endorse guardrails on artificial intelligence, he did push for one change: its name.
Trump said the U.S. would refer in official documents to “superintelligence,” rather than “artificial intelligence.” The word “artificial,” Trump argued, “makes it sound fake, and it is not fake. It’s actually amazing.”
Earlier this month, industry insiders warned that artificial intelligence could lead to human extinction, potentially in the next decade.
Trump said Tuesday that he would not “stifle growth of something that will be bigger than the Industrial Revolution.”
“We’re going to encourage it, not rein it in,” he said. “We’re going to watch it closely through the Department of Justice.”
Trump has previously said that the only guardrail the U.S. needs is “a STRONG AND SMART” president.
Artificial intelligence is also expected to be a main topic of conversation during Trump’s meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping this week.
Greenland, Ukraine and Venezuela
Trump met with several world leaders on the sidelines of the U.N. gathering, including Venezuela’s interim president, Delcy Rodríguez. It was Rodríguez’s first meeting with Trump since the U.S. captured then-Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, who are in a Brooklyn, New York, jail, awaiting trial.
Weeks ago, Trump said that the U.S. entered an agreement with Venezuela for U.S. majority control of more than 65 billion barrels of oil reserves in Venezuela.
On Tuesday, Trump called it “perhaps the biggest deal ever made,” adding: “To the victor belong the spoils.”
Trump said the Venezuela raid was “proof that the United States will no longer permit threats to America to gain a foothold anywhere in the Western Hemisphere,” noting U.S. attacks on drug cartels before pivoting to Cuba.
“My administration is seeking a fundamental change in the situation in Cuba,” he said, adding, “It will fall.”
In response, the Cuban delegation stood up and left the assembly hall.
Later Tuesday, Trump met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who said: “I hope that we will end this war, and President Trump will help us help us end this war,” Zelenskyy said.
Trump said during his speech that the war in Ukraine would end “more quickly than people understand.”
For years, the president said he would end the war. During his 2024 presidential campaign, he said he could end the war within 24 hours or even before his presidency began.
Last week, Trump signed into law a Russian sanctions bill championed by the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C.
He also announced that the U.S. would take over military operations and have “permanent control over security” in Greenland, in a deal signed later Tuesday with the leaders of Greenland and Denmark to try to end the tense standoff over the strategic Arctic territory.

TAINAN, Taiwan (AP) — As China’s Xi Jinping arrives in Washington to meet with U.S. President Donald Trump, Taiwan expressed confidence that U.S. arms sales to the island that Beijing claims as its own will continue — despite China’s pressure.
China has pressed Washington to halt the arms sales, most prominently during a summit in May between Trump and Xi in Beijing. After that meeting, the United States paused the sale of a record-breaking $14 billion package — and Trump described arms sales to Taiwan as a “very good negotiating chip” with China.
Still, the U.S. government and Congress have “repeatedly expressed support for Taiwan’s self-defense capabilities,” Taiwanese Defense Ministry spokesperson Maj. Gen. Chiao Fu-chun told reporters in the southern city of Tainan.
“We will continue to maintain close contact with the U.S. Department of War and continue to push forward the arms procurement deal between Taiwan and the U.S., ensuring it proceeds as planned,” he added.
The U.S. is bound by its own laws to provide Taiwan — a self-ruled democracy that China sees as its own territory — with the means to defend itself. While not recognizing Taiwan as a country, the U.S. is the island’s strongest informal backer and arms provider.
Washington approved another $11 billion package for Taiwan in December.
Hours before Xi’s arrival for the three-day state visit to the U.S., Taiwan’s military on Wednesday conducted live fire drills featuring a domestically developed eight-wheeled armored vehicle, highlighting efforts to strengthen its own arms production.
Called The Cheetah, the vehicle can be fitted with a 105-millimeter (4.1-inch) cannon and can reach a maximum speed of about 100 kph (62 mph) and an operational range of about 500 kilometers (311 miles).
Taiwanese Maj. Gen. Chen Chien-chung said the vehicle can be used on various terrains and is suitable for urban warfare.
Trump has in recent years pressed Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te to dramatically increase Taiwan’s defense budget. The budget will exceed 3% of Taiwan’s gross domestic product for the first time in 2027, and Lai has pledged to get to 5% by 2030.
Mistreanu reported from Taipei, Taiwan.

articles.title_orig: Xi and Trump Seek Safe AI Without Slowing the Race for Supremacy
articles.title_zh: Xi and Trump Seek Safe AI Without Slowing the Race for Supremacy
articles.content_orig:
(Bloomberg) -- Xi Jinping and Donald Trump will sit down this week to hash out a plethora of thorny issues from trade to Taiwan. One thing both sides agree on: neither can afford to tap the brakes on AI.
While Silicon Valley debates the possibility of artificial intelligence wiping out humanity, Washington and Beijing appear more worried about global technological supremacy. The two countries have signaled no intention to slow down AI development — a debate that flared anew after Anthropic PBC co-founder Dario Amodei warned of the dangers of unbridled progress in a 3,800-word communique.
Trump almost immediately dismissed calls for moderation as a "hoax" and vowed to maintain American leadership. Beijing sees little reason to slow down in part because it's already behind the US in AI — though closing the gap — and constrained by American curbs on access to advanced chips by Nvidia Corp.
Just two days before Trump's set to personally greet Xi at a military airbase, Alibaba Group Holding Ltd. declared it was building a mega model of up to 10 trillion parameters, rolling out AI chips it called China's most powerful, and planning a 20-gigawatt data center buildout that could translate into $160 billion of cloud revenue, by one estimate.
That capped a frenetic few days for Chinese AI, with Z.AI Co. and Xiaomi Corp. showcasing how their AI systems improve themselves, and Huawei Technologies Co. accelerating the debut of high-powered AI chips intended to replace Nvidia's processors. Manus – the agentic AI pioneer finally clear of Meta Platforms Inc. – sought to raise capital at a $4 billion valuation to bankroll its next act.
"Neither side wants to give up the development or slow down the development," said Elly Rostoum, a senior fellow with the tech policy program at the Center for European Policy Analysis and a former US intelligence analyst. "But they understand that this is serious enough that they have to talk, that the companies have to talk."
The shared desire by the US and China to push forward suggests Thursday's summit is more likely to produce narrowly defined guardrails rather than speed limits on AI, even as they take tentative steps to build consensus around critical risks. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Washington proposed an emergency hotline for AI incidents and discussed a dialogue mechanism with his Chinese counterparts at a Sunday meeting in New York.
"China already sees itself as being forced to pace because of US tech containment and chip export controls," Selina Xu, who leads China and AI policy research in the office of former Google chief Eric Schmidt, said in an online post. "One remark I've heard from Chinese policymakers is 'we're already being slowed down.'"
To close the gap with the US, China has seized on open-weight AI as a strategy to catch up at home and expand its influence abroad. Beijing is keen to keep up that momentum.
Breakout models such as DeepSeek's R1 and Moonshot's Kimi K3 can be downloaded and adapted by developers worldwide, allowing Chinese laboratories to build on one another's work and squeeze more performance from limited computing resources. This has also won fans overseas and helped embed Chinese software in workflows and products, paving the way for monetization.
Moonshot, for example, is building a team of specialized engineers to help clients deploy and customize models, starting in China before expanding globally. It's also entering commercial partnerships with American cloud providers like Fireworks AI and Baseten to host them.
Z.ai has helped Malaysia build sovereign AI infrastructure, while Saudi Arabia's state-backed Humain commissioned MiniMax Group Inc. to build a national platform based on one of the Chinese startup's open models.
Their popularity — a combination of cost, flexibility and performance — has threatened the ability of leading US AI labs to charge for access to their proprietary offerings. Anthropic and OpenAI have both alleged that Chinese companies use the output from their frontier models to create rival systems at a fraction of the cost, a process known as distillation.
The MiniMax deal drew immediate backlash from US national security hawks. Chris McGuire, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, wrote on X that Washington was "getting played" after agreeing to sell AI chips to Middle Eastern nations on the promise they would rely on an American software stack — only for Saudi Arabia to adopt Chinese technology.
The risk is that these allegations, which Bessent and other officials have echoed, could lead to tougher enforcement of export controls to starve China of the computing resources required to keep up.
The focus on AI risks suggests a shift in emphasis for a rivalry long dominated by US limits on China's access to advanced chips. Export controls remain a major source of tension and may still emerge during Xi's visit, but they have received less attention in the days before his arrival.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said export controls were not on the agenda at his Sunday meeting with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng and chief trade negotiator Li Chenggang. Beijing hasn't confirmed the US account of the exchange, saying only that the two sides discussed AI.
China's continued grip on the global supply of critical minerals likely gives Xi crucial leverage, while Chinese companies including Alibaba accelerate efforts to produce advanced chips that would make the country less vulnerable to Washington's curbs.
But China is not dismissing the technology's dangers altogether. Since ChatGPT's debut in 2022, regulators have introduced rules governing chatbots and proposed restrictions on virtual companions for children. Security officials have also warned about threats of the tools being abused by third parties. This week, the Information reported that China's cyberspace regulators were investigating potential data breaches by Moonshot and DeepSeek, underscoring Beijing's intent to police the industry especially around sensitive content.
Those concerns offer potential common ground with the Trump administration, even if they don't align with the grave risks identified by Amodei and seconded by OpenAI's Sam Altman and SpaceXAI's Elon Musk.
"The existential risk from AI is really not a major topic in China, and not a major topic in the Chinese policymaking world," said Kyle Chan, a fellow with the Brookings Institution. "There's growing convergence in some of the concerns around other major AI risks, namely around cybersecurity, biological weapons, non-state actors."
But any agreement on those areas will have to overcome profound distrust about whether the other side is genuinely addressing safety or merely seeking an advantage.
Amodei has argued that preventing China from gaining an AI edge is paramount for safety, a position he's used to justify tougher export controls. Beijing sees that logic as evidence that calls for safety can serve as a rationale for containment, calling it "fearmongering."
"Cooperation remains limited for the two countries due to low level of trust," said George Chen, a partner at consultancy The Asia Group. Beijing continues to believe Washington is seeking to suppress China's rise in AI and other emerging technologies, a perception that will shape the pace and scope of future engagement, he said.
--With assistance from Luz Ding, Saritha Rai, Rebecca Choong Wilkins and Vlad Savov.

Trump administration accuses banned media outlets of 'falsehoods' ahead of court hearing
The US Justice Department has filed documents that accuse three media outlets banned from the White House of "trafficking in verifiable falsehoods" and reporting which "threatened national security" as it prepared to defend the move in court.
Last week, President Donald Trump barred CNN, Politico and MS NOW from the White House, accusing them of spreading "fake news".
After their reporters had their passes confiscated and were denied access to the building, the three outlets jointly launched legal action, calling the move unconstitutional.
On Wednesday, a judge is set to decide whether to issue an order temporarily lifting the ban, pending a full hearing.
According to a court filing by the Justice Department in a District of Columbia court, the three outlets were issued with a list of "reporting incidents" by the White House ahead of the ban.
The filing cites a number of stories about construction at the White House - including about a security bunker and the building of a new ballroom, as well as a report on an internal information leak investigation.
It goes on to say that "access to the White House is a privilege, not a right".
The three media organisations have argued that the ban breaches their rights under the First Amendment, which forbids the government from "abridging" the freedom of the press.
In a joint statement confirming legal action against the government, they said: "Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists' credentials because it objected to our reporting.
"Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public's right to independent journalism free from government interference."
Major TV networks have withdrawn from a media-sharing arrangement of video and images of the president, known as the pool, in protest over the ban.
Shortly after, the White House launched its own streaming channel, Trump TV, which operates a 24/7 feed of clips of the president.

articles.content_orig:
China's Xi kicks off state visit to Washington on Wednesday with a rare planeside welcome from Trump
When Chinese President Xi Jinping arrives in Washington, he’s expected to get a rare greeting from President Donald Trump, who will be on the tarmac to welcome his counterpart’s plane instead of waiting for him to drive up to the White House
WASHINGTON -- When Chinese President Xi Jinping arrives in Washington on Wednesday, he's expected to get a rare greeting from President Donald Trump, who will be on the tarmac to welcome his counterpart's plane instead of waiting for him to drive up to the White House.
Trump's decision to greet Xi at Joint Base Andrews just outside Washington rather than receiving him at the executive residence shows how far the U.S. president is going to honor China's leader as he makes his first state visit in more than a decade.
The White House has not released many details about Wednesday's greeting, but Trump is expected to participate in an arrival ceremony at the base with Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan. The salutation will kick off a three-day visit that's expected to be saturated with pomp, even by White House standards. The state visit, complete with a formal state dinner at the White House on Thursday, is supposed to reciprocate for the ceremonial grandeur that marked Trump's May visit to China.
But it's also a showy patina at a time when tensions between the two geopolitical rivals are high over trade, artificial intelligence, Trump's war with Iran and China's designs on Taiwan.
Beyond using the visit to try to keep “strategic stability” between the two countries, Trump seems to be pulling out all the diplomatic stops to show off for Xi. He has lavished praise on him as a “great leader” and described a warm relationship with the man he has called a friend. That's all while he's given Xi a pass on many issues.
Mississippi Sen. Roger Wicker, the Republican chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, criticized the “lavish welcome." He said during a speech on the Senate floor on Tuesday that Trump should not have invited the Chinese leader “based on all of the troubling issues we have with President Xi and the Chinese Communist Party.”
Wicker archly suggested a list of topics that Trump could discuss with Xi at the state dinner, such as “the purposes of China’s massive military buildup, or about China’s clear support for Iran,” saying that “during every minute of dialogue” Trump should keep in mind that “his guest is a brutal, unelected and oppressive dictator who seeks to dominate his neighbors and whose massive military arsenal is aimed directly at the United States of America.”
Trump has made it clear he wants to wow Xi, telling reporters in recent weeks that he was delighted his new “work of art” helicopter landing pad would be ready for the visit while bemoaning that his massive White House ballroom would not.
On Wednesday, Trump is expected to try to match the pageantry he was met with in China earlier this year. Xi wasn't there to meet Trump — he sent Chinese Vice President Han Zheng instead. But there was a long red carpet rolled out to meet Air Force One in Beijing. Along the sides were a military honor guard, a military band and about 300 Chinese youths waving Chinese and American flags and chanting, “Welcome, welcome! Warm welcome!” The children were wearing white and light blue uniforms that mirrored the traditional paint colors of the presidential plane.
Trump's airport ceremony will be followed on Thursday by more formalities, including an arrival ceremony at the White House and a review of troops. Before the black-tie dinner — which will feature tech industry leaders like Nvidia’s Jensen Huang and SpaceX’s Elon Musk — the two leaders are expected to dive into the weighty issues behind closed doors, even as expectations are low that the trip will produce any major breakthroughs in the relationship.
On Friday, Xi and Peng will be back at the White House for a private tea with the president and first lady Melania Trump before joining them on a tour of the National Archives in Washington. The White House has said they will view historic documents underscoring the relationship between the two countries.
Associated Press writer Mary Clare Jalonick contributed to this report.

articles.content_orig:
Category 5 Hurricane Polo is 'one of the strongest storms ever'
MEXICO CITY — Hurricane Polo has grown into one of the most powerful Pacific cyclones in decades, and it was expected to skirt Mexico's southwestern coast as a Category 5 storm.
Polo was an "extremely dangerous" storm with maximum sustained winds of 165 mph (265 kph), the Miami-based National Hurricane Center said Tuesday night.
Polo was centered 210 miles (338 kilometers) south of Zihuatanejo, Mexico, and nearly stationary over the Pacific Ocean. The hurricane center said Polo was expected to start a slow but sharp turn northwest during the night and then travel in a generally west-northwestward direction over the next several days.
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said experts indicated that the hurricane was not likely to touch land. Still, the NHC said hurricane-force winds are happening up to 40 miles (65 kilometers) from the storm's center and tropical storm-force winds up to 105 miles (169 kilometers) away.
The hurricane set residents along Mexico's Pacific coast on edge once again after being walloped by powerful cyclones a number of times in recent years. Beaches emptied out and dark clouds swirled above choppy seas, while Mexican authorities temporarily suspended classes Tuesday in a number of areas. Mexico's navy shut down ports in the states of Guerrero and Michoacán and warned civilians and fishermen to take care.
Waves, flooding and mudslides are all risks
Concepción López Villegas was busily preparing her seaside restaurant for what may come. Strong waves were already lapping at the coastline of her city Lázaro Cárdenas in Michoacán. As men and children watched the stirring waters behind her, López Villegas said she feared powerful waves would destroy the small business she has worked decades to build.
"We're worried and trying to protect our businesses," López Villegas said. "And of course, we're sad because it's our heritage, our legacy that from one moment to another could be destroyed."
National Hurricane Center data shows that Polo has reached speeds comparable to only a few hurricanes to form in the region in recent decades, primarily Hurricane Patricia, which reached 215 mph (346 kph) in 2015.
"This is one of the strongest storms ever in the (Pacific) Basin," said Kristen L. Corbosiero, professor at the University at Albany's Department of Atmospheric & Environmental Sciences.
The NHC warned that tropical storm conditions were expected along the Pacific coast in Guerrero, Michoacan and Colima states.
Heavy rain could produce flash flooding and mudslides. About 3 to 6 inches (8 to 15 centimeters) of rain was forecast for Guerrero and Michoacán states, with smaller amounts possible for coastal portions of Oaxaca, Colima and Jalisco states.
El Niño fueled rapid intensification
The U.S. Embassy in Mexico issued a weather alert, instructing citizens to avoid water and beaches and to heed warnings from Mexican authorities.
"Even if the storm does not make direct landfall, heavy rain may produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides. Hazardous ocean conditions—intensified by storms—may result in deadly rip currents and rogue waves," the embassy wrote in a statement.
The rapid intensification of the storm has stunned scientists and authorities alike, with the NHC writing in a report that it was "truly remarkable" how quickly Polo gained strength in the past 24 hours.
Philip Klotzbach, research scientist in the Department of Atmospheric Science at Colorado State University, attributed the intensification to the weather phenomenon known as El Niño, which has fueled crippling droughts in Mexico and Central America and floods in other parts of the region.
In the Pacific, it has resulted in warmer waters and wind patterns that act as fodder for hurricanes, he said.
"There are all the ingredients that hurricanes need to get really strong really fast," Klotzbach said.
Polo is the third Category 5 hurricane of the Pacific season, following Genevieve and Lowell earlier this year. Category 5 is the highest level on the Saffir-Simpson scale, reflecting that a storm has maximum sustained winds exceeding 157 mph (253 kph).
No Atlantic hurricanes have formed yet this year, and this year has set a record for the longest start to a season without a hurricane. The effects of this year's El Niño crush storms before they get going.

Donald Trump Says He Could ‘Annihilate’ Iran After Touting Peace Efforts
President Donald Trump told the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday that he could "annihilate" Iran if the nearly seven-month war does not end in a deal, even as he cast himself as a peacemaker working to close out multiple global wars. The remarks, given in New York, came alongside a day of intense back-channel diplomacy between US and Iranian officials.
Donald Trump's Iran remarks come during United Nations speech
Trump to the UN: "Do I annihilate the Islamic Republic, and do it quickly? Do I drive them into hell?" pic.twitter.com/cIYBO1Mp3w
— Aaron Rupar (@atrupar) September 22, 2026
Speaking before a packed hall, Trump said he faced a stark choice. "I have a big decision to make," he said. "Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before?… Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again? Do I drive them into hell?" Only a single member of Iran's delegation was present to watch the speech.
Trump used much of his address to defend the US-Israeli military campaign against Iran, arguing the war had stopped Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon and proved the value of what he called peace through strength. He also touted efforts to broker peace between Russia and Ukraine, rejected the idea of "global government," and pledged that the US would win the global race on artificial intelligence.
His tone stood in contrast to UN Secretary-General António Guterres, who had earlier warned that global divisions were increasing and stressed the interdependence of nations. According to Reuters, Iran's Armed Forces rejected Donald Trump's UN remarks as "propaganda" in a statement Tuesday, warning of "full readiness to inflict more severe, crushing, and unpredictable blows on the aggressors."
Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf, who led Iran's negotiating team in earlier talks, said Tehran would not bow to pressure: "Trump must understand that he cannot impose his power on the Iranian people and its armed forces." Despite the threats exchanged publicly, US and Iranian officials continued diplomatic contacts Tuesday, including discussions through mediators and a meeting on the sidelines of the UN gathering.

articles.title_zh: Dolly Parton’s estate accuses her nephew of threatening violence and to destroy his aunt’s legacy
articles.content_orig:
The estate of the late Dolly Parton is involved in a dispute with the country star’s nephew and former head of security, and has filed for a restraining order against him amid allegations of threats.
Bryan Seaver was responsible for Parton’s security, and was tasked with announcing her death on 25 August with a video, “something Dolly asked of me years ago”, he said.
But since the singer died, her estate, which is run by Parton’s manager Danny Nozell, has reportedly fired Seaver from his security job, and has now alleged that he made “relentless” threats against Nozell and others.
According to Billboard, the lawsuit filed in a Tennessee court reads: “These were not ordinary workplace disputes or heated words; they were deliberate threats from a self-proclaimed heavily armed, former security operative with a military-contractor background. Many of [Parton’s staff members] are now afraid to come to work or have resigned entirely because they do not feel safe.”
Seaver is alleged to have written to a lawyer for Parton, “I’m a killer”, and separately told Nozell: “I’m literally an international arms dealer and mercenary. All I do is warfare. Everyone needs to be worried about what I might do.” He is also alleged to have claimed that he made a $27m arms and ammunition deal with Haiti.
He allegedly claimed he would “set up a podcast dedicated to ruining Dolly’s brand partnerships and telling the violations these people have done on us. It’s going to be great. Or fucking pay me.”
Seaver repeated some of those claims in comments to TMZ while defending his actions, saying: “I am a career soldier and military contractor and do conduct arms deals for foreign governments. I am a security professional and I am a killer. However, nothing in this lawsuit were threats and most of the comments I stand by.”
Regarding the messages to Nozell, Seaver said: “I was talking frankly in a private way with Danny who I thought was my friend and he fancies himself a gangster. A lot of these messages are two guys having rage talk and crying on the phone together while we were grieving.”
In another message, Seaver reportedly said: “I’m going to spend the next times I have on earth ratfucking anyone that has ever betrayed my family.”
Speaking to TMZ, Seaver said of that comment: “I was talking about people that have done bad to Dolly in business – a specific company that scared her and intimated her. Those comments were about specific, horrible business partners that have done wrong to her and I stand by that.”
Seaver’s security contract was terminated on 15 September, with a leaked termination letter saying the decision was made “for the protection of the trust and beneficiaries as a whole”, though it reassured Seaver it was “not a termination of your personal interest in the trust”.
Seaver put out a statement after the termination, saying: “We remain unshakably resolved to fulfil her final directive to protect her family, and we refuse to be intimidated by those whose actions we believe are being taken in bad faith and with the intent to profit from the life of someone who willingly gave so much.”
The chancery court in Nashville will now consider the restraining order filing. The Guardian has contacted Seaver and lawyers for Parton’s estate for further comment.
Parton left behind considerable financial assets: not only her songbook featuring hits such as 9 to 5, but also a broad business empire including the entertainment resort Dollywood in Tennessee.
She had no children, and her husband, Carl, died in 2025, but she is survived by other family members including six siblings and an uncle. Seaver is the son of her sister Cassie.
