O n Sunday, just as polling closed in Russia ’s parliamentary elections, Ukraine launched one of its biggest drone strikes on Moscow since the war broke out over four years ago.
Striking images from the city showed a large refinery in flames and vast plumes of smoke billowing from chimneys . Over 450 drones were shot down in what the region’s mayor Sergei Sobyanin called “the most massive” attack it had seen.
The attacks came shortly after US president Donald Trump had ordered both sides to quit their attacks on energy infrastructure. But both countries have continued to attack each other despite the pleas.
According to a report by the International Energy Association , all but five of Russia’s 32 major oil refineries have escaped attack since war broke out, while some have been hit up to 15 times.
Those unaffected currently lie outside of the reach of Ukraine’s most advanced drones, between 3,500km and 6,500km from the border in eastern Siberia or the far east of the country.
The IEA has said that this strategy has intensified significantly over the past 18 months so that by June, throughput fell to its lowest level in more than 20 years and 30 per cent blow a year earlier.
Gasoline output has dropped by 20 per cent compared to 2024, while diesel production has fallen by nearly 30 per cent.
The attacks have led to images being released from Russia that will be unnerving for Russian leader Vladimir Putin : huge queues at fuelling stations (lasting up to 40 hours, according to some motorists), and rising oil and gas prices.
Fuel shortages have been reported across 92 per cent of Russia’s regions with around two-third introducing fuel-rationing measures.
The crisis has forced the Russian government to restrict oil exports to protect domestic supplies.
Ukraine’s military suggests that Russia’s total oil refining capacity is down by 45 per cent, according to a report by the General Staff released on Monday.
“Ukraine is increasingly using multiple waves of drones against individual refineries, seeking to overwhelm protective netting and other largely passive drone defence measures,” wrote the IEA.
“Its long-range capabilities and targeting have also advanced rapidly, particularly during the first half of 2026. This expanded reach enabled the 7 July strike on Gazprom Neft’s 450 thousand barrels per day (kb/d) Omsk refinery, Russia’s largest, roughly 2,500 kilometres from the Ukrainian border.”
The IEA says that there has not been “significant damage” reported to both primary and secondary crude oil processing units across the country.
As Ukraine becomes effective at striking the refineries it is “increasingly targeting specific refinery units to maximise the impact of each strike”.
It explained that Kyiv targets crude distillation units (CDUs), where the crude is initially processed, as well as secondary units such as fluid catalytic crackers (FCCs), hydrocrackers, reformers and hydrotreaters.
While damage to CDUs can typically be repaired within a week or two, damage to the more complex secondary units can take six to eight months to fix on average.
Russia has been forced to deal with the crisis by rationing fuel and also allowing the production of lower quality energy, allowing higher-sulphur grades of gasoline to be produced for the first time since 2016.
In May, the Washington Post reported that more than 20 strikes on Russian oil infrastructure in 2026 had cost Moscow over $7bn.
The Ukrainians have hit almost all the major refineries in European Russia and the Urals at least once. They have also damaged the country’s largest refinery located in Omsk (Siberia),” says John Lough, head of foreign policy at the New Eurasian Strategies Centre (NEST).
“It’s very difficult to put a figure on the total losses incurred through damage to refineries, lost production and overall disruption. It’s probably around $20 billion.”
But the picture is more complex as analysis by Reuters in July found that Russia’s oil and gas revenue had increased 60 per cent compared to the year before due to the increase in global oil prices.
The loss of oil prices is also putting further pressure on global oil supplies already squeezed due to the ongoing war in Iran , which has seen the Strait of Hormuz largely shut since March.
Whether the strategy has been effective in the long-run therefore may depend on multiple factors.
But Lough says that “its main value is psychological since it has brought the war home to Russians who were previously insulated from it and made them think about why the country is so poorly defended when the war was supposed to improve Russia’s security.”
“It’s hardly a coincidence that the authorities had to remove the Yabloko party from last weekend’s Duma elections. It was the only party campaigning for ending the war against Ukraine,” he added.
“It was supposed to receive only a tiny proportion of the vote, but the authorities concluded that its message risked resonating among the electorate.
“For Ukraine, it has been a double-edged sword. Russia has stepped up its own air campaign and has stopped the operation of the Black Sea ports – a lifeline for the Ukrainian economy. It has also intensified its attacks on other economic assets across the country.”

articles.title_zh: Trump administration to remove 760,000 Affordable Care Act enrollees over fraud claims
articles.content_orig:
Trump administration to remove 760,000 Affordable Care Act enrollees over fraud claims
WASHINGTON — Vice President JD Vance and other Trump administration officials said Tuesday they plan to remove 760,000 Affordable Care Act enrollees from public healthcare exchanges, alleging that the individuals were fraudulently enrolled in the program, or simply do not exist.
Vance said the discovery and canceled subsidy payments for hundreds of thousands of people from the exchanges, part of an administration-wide crackdown on fraud, would result in $2.2 billion in cost savings.
"We're actually making sure that the people receiving Obamacare subsidies are actually entitled to receive them," said Vance, who leads a government task force to eliminate fraud. He was flanked by Dr. Mehmet Oz, the administrator for the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, or CMS, and other administration officials.
Vance said the cancellation of approximately 315,000 enrollments covering 760,000 people was done in part because the government was not checking whether people enrolled were eligible. Vance said another 419,000 enrollments will get additional verification to make sure they are eligible for the benefit.
The Trump administration also announced a six-month suspension on new agents or brokers who sign up enrollees for healthcare coverage, who officials say commit a disproportionate amount of the fraud they uncovered.
Roughly 19.2 million Americans are actively enrolled in ACA marketplace health plans as of early 2026, according to the Department of Health and Human Services website. The number of enrollees grew during the COVID-19 pandemic when enhanced subsidies became available through the American Rescue Plan Act and Inflation Reduction Act, both signed into law by former President Joe Biden.
Tuesday's announcement is the latest in an initiative by the Trump administration to address fraud around the country, including in federal healthcare programs, which officials say is needed to rein in runaway spending and protect taxpayers.
Some healthcare policy experts are calling for more transparency on how the Trump administration decided to cut hundreds of thousands of enrollees — and question how many people may have been wrongly cut from the program.
Cynthia Cox, a vice president and director of the ACA program at the healthcare research nonprofit KFF, said "I think there's no question that somebody who was fraudulently enrolled should have their coverage canceled," however, "I think the question is whether this was the appropriate process by which to identify fraudulent enrollees, and also whether all of them were indeed fraudulently enrolled."
Cox said the elimination of the people from ACA programs was done outside of the normal regulatory process.
Ellen Montz, a former deputy administrator and director at the Center for Consumer Information and Insurance Oversight at CMS during the Biden administration said during her time in government, there was an ongoing effort to eliminate fraud from ACA programs.
"There's a lot of work to be done, and the Trump administration has done some good things that are targeting the actual fraudsters," she said. Adding that Tuesday's announcement lacked details on how the administration determined who to cut. " I would imagine we'll hear from some subset of consumers that ask: why did my enrollment get cancelled?" Montz said.
At the press conference, Tuesday, Vance referred to some enrollments lacking social security numbers or immigration documentation.
The announcement comes as stubbornly high inflation and rising healthcare costs pressure the Trump administration to come up with a plan to bring down costs for Americans as affordability remains a central issue in the fall midterm elections.
The price of ACA insurance has skyrocketed for many Americans during Trump's second term, after Republicans opposed extending COVID-era subsidies that had helped offset the costs of health insurance for most enrollees during Biden's term.
Premiums doubled or tripled for many enrollees, prompting millions to downgrade their plans or exit the program entirely after the Republican-led Congress allowed the subsidies to expire this year.
The Government Accountability Office suggests fraud risks in the advance premium tax credit do exist - however it's unclear at what scale. The GAO conducted covert testing using fictitious ACA applicants enrolled in 2024 and 2025. A report released in December showed that the federal marketplace approved subsidized coverage for almost all of the GAO's 24 fake enrollees.
The White House referred The Associated Press to the Vice President's team for additional comment on bigger plans to address healthcare affordability. The Vice President's office and CMS did not respond to Associated Press requests for comment.
The Wall Street Journal first reported the news of the Trump administration's plan to remove ACA enrollees from public exchanges.
Democratic lawmakers criticized the move to remove enrollees from ACA coverage.
Richard E. Neal, a Massachusetts Democrat and ranking member of the Ways and Means Committee, said "Republicans have already created the worst healthcare crisis ever, but every decision by the Trump Administration is designed to keep making it worse."
"As if making coverage harder to access through skyrocketing premiums and more red tape wasn't painful enough, they're doubling down to take it away entirely," Neal said.

Venezuelan interim President Delcy Rodríguez shared details Tuesday about her “historic meeting” with President Trump on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly.
The pull-aside took place at a Trump-hosted reception at the Lotte Palace Hotel in New York and marked the first meeting between the two leaders since US forces captured and deposed former Venezuelan dictator Nicolas Maduro in January.
“We held a historic meeting with the President of the United States, Donald Trump, with whom we discussed strengthening the bilateral relationship between our countries and advancing a cooperation agenda in strategic areas such as energy, mining, and security and other matters of common interest,” Rodríguez wrote on X, including a photo of herself standing next to the commander-in-chief.
The Venezuelan leader, who previously served as Maduro’s vice president, said she expressed her “gratitude” for the Trump administration’s “resolute support” in the aftermath of a devastating June 24 earthquake, as well as for “their backing of the reintegration process of our country in multilateral spaces.”
“Venezuela and the United States share a historical relationship that, in this new stage, we are called to channel through dialogue,” Rodríguez continued. “We will continue to promote a diplomacy at the service of the national interest, oriented toward achieving concrete results and collective benefits for the Venezuelan people.”
Trump was joined at the meeting by Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, chief of staff Susie Wiles and deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller, according to the White House.
Meanwhile, Rodríguez reportedly brought her vice president of economy, oil minister and officials from state oil company PDVSA, sources told Reuters.
In his UN speech earlier Tuesday, Trump touted the release of hundreds of Venezuelan political prisoners and the massive oil deal struck with the South American nation as tangible results since the daring, middle-of-the-night raid on “outlaw dictator” Maduro’s compound.
“To the victor belong the spoils,” the president declared, describing the oil agreement inked with Caracas last month as “perhaps the biggest deal ever made.”
Trump indicated that he’s aiming for some $100 billion in investment to flow into Venezuela’s oil industry as part of the deal, which grants the US control of more than 65 billion barrels of proven oil reserves in the socialist country.

articles.title_orig: White House Defends Trump’s Ban on CNN, MS NOW and Politico in Court Filing
articles.title_zh: White House Defends Trump’s Ban on CNN, MS NOW and Politico in Court Filing
articles.content_orig:
CNN, MS NOW and Politico sue to restore White House access
Washington — CNN, MS NOW and Politico announced Monday that the news organizations are suing the Trump administration over President Trump's ban of the news outlets from the White House, arguing the ban was unconstitutional on First Amendment grounds.
Mr. Trump said Friday in a Truth Social post that he was barring CNN, MS Now, and Politico from the White House, in the Trump administration's latest move to target news outlets for what he views as disfavorable coverage.
In a joint statement on Monday, the three news organizations said they are suing to immediately restore access after they were denied entry on Saturday and had their press passes revoked.
"There could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment," the legal motion from the news organizations said. "Presidents from the earliest days of the Republic have disagreed with and complained about the tenor and content of press coverage of their administrations."
Mr. Trump posted on social media on Monday morning that the White House "is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish. It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America." He also wrote in a separate social media post, "FAKE NEWS IS A THREAT TO DEMOCRACY, and I will do whatever is necessary to make sure that the U.S.A. thrives."
The case was assigned to U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, who was appointed to the federal bench by Mr. Trump during his first term. Kelly oversaw a lawsuit brought by former CNN reporter Jim Acosta during the first Trump administration after the White House moved to revoke his access. The judge sided with Acosta after CNN sued and ordered his press pass to be restored, finding Acosta's due process rights under the Fifth Amendment had been violated. The White House obeyed the order.
Kelly scheduled a hearing on the CNN/MS NOW/Politico suit for Wednesday afternoon, and the Justice Department replied late Tuesday to the suit, saying the ban was at least partly on national security grounds.
The department argued that Kelly should deny the news organizations' motion to restore their access to the White House because "the President concluded that they have failed to maintain basic minimum 'standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House Complex, including' by 'publishing sensitive or classified information.' ... In response, the president has preliminarily revoked their continued access to White House grounds. ... After all, access to the White House is a privilege — not a right."
The Trump administration, the DOJ said, is giving the outlets until Sept. 25 at 5 p.m. to contest the decision to revoke access.
The lawsuit is asking a Washington, D.C., judge to move quickly to prevent further action from the White House on the ban. CNN was scheduled to be traveling with the president on Monday as the network pool team. Without a replacement, there was no television network traveling with Mr. Trump — an unprecedented move.
The motion says they have notified the Trump administration of their intent to sue. The lawsuit names Mr. Trump and three of his top aides — Susie Wiles, the White House chief of staff, as well as spokesperson Steven Cheung and Secret Secret chief Sean Curran.
Speaking to reporters after the announcement on Friday, Mr. Trump said there is "no reason" why the ban was issued when it was, and suggested it wasn't in response to any specific incident.
"I don't think somebody should be allowed to come and write fake stories. They're fake news. And they have no credibility," Mr. Trump said. "Now, if they want to write them, that's fine, but I don't have to let them into my — into the people's house."
Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press President Bruce Brown called the ban "flatly unconstitutional." He said the decision to block the outlets from White House grounds was "textbook viewpoint discrimination and will be quickly struck down by the courts if challenged."
The administration curbed news outlets' access to the Pentagon last year. The Defense Department required journalists with daily access to the building to sign onto a slew of rules, including one that suggested reporters who "solicit" sensitive information could be deemed a security risk and kicked out of the Pentagon. Most news outlets — including CBS News, ABC News, NBC News, Fox News and CNN — declined to sign and left the Pentagon.
After a judge struck down some of those rules earlier this year, the Defense Department changed course and began requiring any reporters on Pentagon grounds to be escorted by government personnel. An appeals court allowed that policy to remain in place.
In its response to the CNN/MS NOW/Politico suit late Tuesday, the DOJ included two sworn statements, one from Kingsley Lewis, the Pentagon press secretary, and the other from a top Pentagon official, claiming that after the Pentagon limited media access, leaks have slowed, and the same would happen if the White House ban is allowed to proceed.
The Trump administration has made other attempts to remove media outlets from the White House and other spaces.
Last year, Mr. Trump barred The Associated Press from attending certain White House events after the news outlet refused to conform to Mr. Trump's proclamation that the Gulf of Mexico was now the "Gulf of America."
The wire service sued on First Amendment grounds shortly afterwards, and while a federal judge in D.C. initially ruled that the White House must restore the news outlet's access, an appeals court later allowed the ban to take effect.
The appellate ruling hinged on the fact that the AP was blocked from certain restricted spaces like the Oval Office and Air Force One that only a small subset of the White House press corps can access — a narrower policy than the outright ban imposed on CNN, MS NOW and Politico. The appeals court judges said the White House can't ban journalists from spaces that are "generally open to the press," like the briefing room, based on their viewpoint.
As the legal process played out, the White House assumed control of the press pool, a small, rotating group of journalists who cover the president every day and disseminate information and footage to other news outlets. The print press pool works in rotation so that wire outlets, including the AP, are now not granted access to spaces like Air Force One or the Oval Office as frequently as they once were.

Ella Langley speaks out after breaking Mariah Carey’s record for longest-running No. 1 of all time
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Ella Langley credited her hit song “Choosin’ Texas” for “changing her life” after she broke Mariah Carey’s record for the longest run at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100.
“I’m genuinely trying to find the words to help explain what’s going on in my brain today,” Langley, 27, said on Tuesday in an Instagram video posted from beside her pool just hours after the record was announced.
“Choosin’ Texas” has spent 23 weeks atop the chart since February, surpassing Carey’s 1994 hit “All I Want for Christmas Is You,” which held the record at 22 weeks, accumulated across the holiday seasons from 2019 through 2026.
“Thank you so much. Thank you for loving this song. For listening to it. I don’t even know what to say at this point. I’m running out of hyperboles to describe how I feel, so I will just let my dog in the background show you his excitement,” Langley continued.
The country star joked she was waiting to be pranked.
“It’s changing my life. It’s changing the lives of the writers of this song. It’s changing the lives of my family and it is truly growing in atmosphere for something I’m going to be able to do for the rest of my life,” she said.
“It doesn’t feel like a real thing. It feels fake and somebody is going to come and say, ‘Haha, we’re kidding the whole time.’”
“I’m going to go out and celebrate tonight and I’m really excited to just experience a moment like this in my life,” she added.
“Choosin’ Texas” debuted on the Hot 100 in November 2025 and became Langley’s first top 10 hit in January before reaching No. 1 in February. The song has now spent 48 weeks on the chart overall, Billboard reported.
The Hot 100 combines US streaming, radio airplay and sales data across all genres.
The song, which Langley co-wrote alongside Luke Dick, Miranda Lambert and Joybeth Taylor, collected 21.8 million official streams in the latest tracking week, down 9 percent from the previous week, while its radio audience rose 2 percent to 58.3 million impressions.
It is also in the top 10 on the pop airplay, adult-pop airplay and adult contemporary charts.
But Langley’s record could face a challenge from Carey when Christmas arrives.
“All I Want for Christmas Is You,” released in 1994, has returned to No. 1 during the holiday season every year since it first topped the Hot 100 in 2019.
The closest songs to Langley and Carey on the all-time Hot 100 leaderboard are Shaboozey’s “A Bar Song (Tipsy)” from 2024 and Lil Nas X’s “Old Town Road,” featuring Billy Ray Cyrus, from 2019, which each spent 19 weeks at No. 1.
Langley also appeared to take a stab at Doja Cat last month after the rapper was asked during an appearance on the “Sundae Conversation” podcast if she was a fan of Langley.
“I don’t know what that is,” Doja said, to which Langley later posted, “Ella Langley? What is that?”

Trump Administration officials on Tuesday announced that they would terminate the Obamacare coverage of 760,000 enrollees, alleging widespread fraud in enrollment.
Vice President JD Vance, who leads a White House task force aimed at eliminating fraud, said while speaking to reporters that $2.2 billion in taxpayer funds would be saved by removing the hundreds of thousands of Affordable Care Act (ACA) enrollees from the public insurance marketplaces.
“We expect that most of these people are fraudulently enrolled,” Vance said. He added that the Administration would also work to verify the eligibility of roughly 419,000 additional enrollees by ensuring that they are legal residents of the U.S. and meet the income threshold to receive Obamacare coverage.
The Administration will also place a six month moratorium on new health insurance brokers and agents, who help individuals sign up for health plans, Vance said.
Read More: Trump Pledges to Issue $500 Refunds to Nearly a Million Obamacare Enrollees. Are You Eligible?
The Administration’s move to eject fraudulent enrollees from the Obamacare insurance marketplaces is the latest in its broader efforts to crack down on fraud. An online “ledger” maintained by the White House asserts that the Vance-led anti-fraud task force has uncovered nearly $250 billion worth of fraud since Trump returned to office last January, including almost $100 billion at the Department of Health and Human Services.
That crackdown also saw the Administration pause $867.5 million in Medicaid payments to California and $199 million in Minnesota in July, an action for which Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. cited “suspected fraud and noncompliance.” Both states have pushed back on the claims.
The Administration has additionally targeted alleged fraud in food stamps , childcare facilities, COVID-era relief funding, student loans, and homelessness funding, among other areas. Critics have accused it of disproportionally focusing on Democratic-led states in its crackdown.
An analysis from the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) released last August estimated that 2.3 million Obamacare enrollees improperly claimed premium tax credits by intentionally overstating their income in 2025. The Trump Administration has also claimed that agents and brokers have been responsible for illegally enrolling tens of thousands of people in ACA plans.
The 760,000 enrollees now being removed from the ACA rolls by the Trump Administration represent about 4% of the estimated 19.2 million people receiving coverage through the marketplaces in 2026.
That total has sharply declined from its peak of more than 24 million last year as ACA premiums have surged following the expiration of subsidies that helped reduce costs for millions of enrollees at the end of 2025.
A poll conducted by health policy research group KFF in June found that most voters believe there is at least some fraud in government health programs, and that more than 70% feel it is an extremely or very important issue for candidates to discuss ahead of the midterm elections. For Republican voters, fraud topped all health care issues asked about in the survey, including costs.
But health care costs, which have become increasingly expensive in the U.S. in recent years, weighed more significantly for voters overall, and the poll found that only a minority of those surveyed believed that reducing fraud in government programs would reduce such costs for them personally.
Amid the Trump Administration’s moves to withhold millions in Medicaid payments, 71% also voiced the belief that preserving access to coverage through the insurance program was more important than rooting out fraud. Meanwhile, 65% believed that the Administration’s Medicaid payment deferrals were mostly politically motivated.

Men’s title a landmark achievement for China, with success marking the 200th gold in athletics at the regional multi-sport event
China’s racewalkers secured a landmark gold as they dominated the half marathons at the Asian Games on Wednesday, winning both the men’s and women’s events.
A new distance compared to the 20km version contested at previous Asian Games, Shi Shengji stormed to the men’s title at the Aichi-Nagoya race walking course in one hour, 23 minutes and 32 seconds.

AUSTIN, Texas — The ICE officer who shot a Venezuelan man in Austin on Sunday, leaving a bullet lodged in his back, was issued a body camera but was not wearing it during the shooting, two officials with the Department of Homeland Security told NBC News.
The officials said it was not clear why the officer was not wearing his body camera. Another ICE officer who was in the same vehicle was wearing a body camera, the officials said. That camera captured partial footage of the incident, but the footage does not include the moment of the shooting, the officials said.
Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, 28, was shot early Sunday afternoon by an ICE officer while making deliveries as a DoorDash driver. He was taken to a hospital and, four hours after he was shot, was taken into immigration custody at the South Texas ICE Processing Center in Pearsall, Texas, his attorney said. The bullet remains in his back.
On Tuesday, a federal judge granted an emergency order temporarily blocking deportation proceedings against Garcés Pérez, according to his attorney, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch.
The Travis County District Attorney’s Office also sent a letter to DHS and ICE leadership requesting that Garcés Pérez be allowed to remain in the country since he is “a material witness” in their criminal investigation into the shooting.
Austin Police Chief Lisa Davis shared on Tuesday evening some of the first video footage obtained by the department as part on their probe into the shooting. The videos came from an off-duty officer who captured part of the encounter between ICE and Garcés Pérez, as well as the sound of three gunshots, using his personal dash cam and cellphone.
After this, the off-duty officer alerted his colleagues to the shooting, allowing Austin police to quickly respond to the scene.
Davis said they are seeking the public’s help in obtaining any video evidence that can help them piece together the pursuit that preceded the shooting.
The day after he was shot, Garcés Pérez began “experiencing an inability to move his arm,” attorney Lincoln-Goldfinch said on social media. He was taken to the hospital Monday afternoon for several hours and then sent back to the detention center, she said.
The DHS did not respond to requests for comment about Lincoln-Goldfinch’s statements.
Earlier Monday, Garcés Pérez told a news conference via phone from detention that he was in a lot of pain and wasn’t getting the medical care he needed.
Lincoln-Goldfinch alleged in a social media post that after Garcés Pérez spoke out at the news conference, guards at the detention center “forcibly took the tablet from his hands, revoked his communication privileges, and moved him out of the infirmary into an isolated room with a flat bed that cannot be adjusted like a medical bed.”
He was then taken to the hospital around 5 p.m. after losing his ability to move his arm, she said.
“Wilber reports that he was handcuffed, shackled at the ankles, placed in a waist chain, and handled roughly during that transfer,” she said in the post.
Lincoln-Goldfinch said Garcés Pérez told her on Tuesday morning that doctors spoke to him about his care and gave him morphine for his pain.
“We now understand that the gunshot fractured his clavicle and that he has significant swelling and is wearing a sling,” she wrote. “We still do not have clarity about the cause or extent of the loss of movement he experienced.”
The attorney said Garcés Pérez was discharged from the hospital around midnight and taken back to the detention center, where he is receiving Tylenol and ibuprofen for his ongoing pain.
“He remains in isolation, on a flat bed, and without the tablet he previously used to communicate,” she said.
“We are asking for his communication privileges to be immediately restored and for him to be provided an appropriate medical bed and adequate medical care,” she said. “Most importantly, we are continuing to advocate for Wilber’s IMMEDIATE release.”
Rep. Joaquin Castro, D-Texas, said on social media that “despite losing movement on his left side and having a bullet lodged next to his spine, ICE has forced Wilber Rafael out of the hospital and back to the South Texas ICE Processing Center in Pearsall, Texas.”
He said that he and Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, would visit Garcés Pérez on Wednesday, check on his condition and demand his release.
A DHS spokesperson said in a statement late Sunday that Garcés Pérez was in stable condition and was in federal custody pending removal from the U.S.
A senior administration official told NBC News on Monday that Garcés Pérez did not have a criminal history beyond being in the country illegally.
According to Lincoln-Goldfinch, Garcés Pérez entered the country legally and was seeking asylum. She said Garcés Pérez had filed a change of address in immigration court, but received a notice to appear in court at the old address and never got it. Because he missed his immigration hearing, Garcés Pérez was ordered deported in absentia, according to his attorney.
On Monday, Lincoln-Goldfinch shared Garcés Pérez’s account of the shooting, saying he was making a delivery when “an unmarked black truck sideswiped him.” She said he didn’t know it was ICE as the truck chased him as he tried to make a U-turn, and then “pulled him out of the car.”
Previously, DHS has accused immigrants involved in shootings with ICE of using their cars as weapons while fleeing agents, without offering evidence of its claims. But it did not make the accusation in the case of Garcés Pérez or in the case of Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, who was fatally shot in Biddeford, Maine, in July during a traffic stop.
ICE Director David Venturella previously told NBC News that every ICE officer and agent would be equipped with body cameras by the end of August, adding the agency would allow the “expedited release” of bodycam footage “when appropriate.” Further delaying that timeline is the possibility of DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin potentially switching or adding new vendors for body cameras.
A person who witnessed the aftermath of the shooting but who requested anonymity because he is going through immigration proceedings told Noticias Telemundo that he was waiting on customers at the ice cream shop where he works when he heard gunshots and ran outside, where he saw immigration agents surrounding a car.
“I approached the car and saw a man who looked sad and with his eyes full of tears. I asked him what happened to him, and he just told me, ‘I was shot in the back,’” said the person, a Mexican immigrant who has lived in the U.S. for more than two decades.
“You aren’t prepared to see someone like that. It makes you very angry, it pains you and you don’t know what to do,” he said.
A social media video verified by NBC News captures the sound of tires screeching followed by a person exiting a dark-colored SUV as a blue sedan is stopped next to it, both vehicles facing each other. The sedan appears to be damaged on the passenger side.
At least three gunshots are heard as the person approaches the sedan and runs up to it as it slowly lurches forward. The video shows the person standing next to the sedan’s driver’s side as it stops in front of an intersection.
Another video shows the blue sedan with its driver’s side door open and Garcés Pérez hunched over in the driver’s seat, holding his left upper chest, near his shoulder, as multiple law enforcement officers gather around.
The woman taking the video says, “Why did he do that to him?” The officers tell her that an ambulance is coming.
The video shows Garcés Pérez being taken out of the car and handcuffed behind his back. The agents make him sit on the ground. There appears to be a large bloodstain down his back. The officers cut open the back of his shirt, revealing a bullet hole.
An officer asks the woman taking the video if she saw what happened. In Spanish, she replies that “they just shot him because he didn’t want to stop” his vehicle.

得克萨斯州奥斯汀——新视频揭示了周日北奥斯汀ICE枪击案的筹备情况，尽管关键时刻仍然缺失。
奥斯汀警方发布了一段视频，显示ICE特工在枪击事件发生前与威尔伯·加西斯·佩雷斯的蓝色汽车在一起，以及随后执法部门的反应。然而，该视频不包括枪声或从最初停止到拍摄之间的10-15分钟。
相关| ICE参与北奥斯汀枪击案后，居民聚集在一起纪念
一名下班的奥斯汀警探恰好在附近，在进入附近的一家购物中心之前，用Garcés Pérez的个人行车记录仪在他的车辆附近抓获了ICE特工。据奥斯汀警察局官员称，在接下来的10到15分钟内，有一辆车在附近的街区被追赶，但该部门澄清说，没有证据表明有人徒步追赶。
奥斯汀警察局长丽莎·戴维斯说：“我们有一些视频，我们正在处理一段经过那里一些街区的追捕视频，并在那里结束。”。
警方表示，这段时间的视频是存在的，调查人员仍在努力收集和处理。目前尚不清楚的是，加西亚·佩雷斯为什么离开最初的交通站，沿途发生了什么事件，以及导致立交桥下发生枪击事件的原因。
Garcés Pérez的律师表示，她的客户报告称被一辆黑色SUV追赶，最初没有意识到这辆车属于执法部门。她说他正试图到达一个更安全的地方，而不是试图逃跑。
APD发布了关于北奥斯汀ICE枪杀委内瑞拉男子的视频
当休班的侦探回到车上时，他开始用手机录音，听到了三声枪响。现场第一名奥斯汀警察的随身摄像机镜头显示了枪击事件后的反应，但发布的视频中没有一段包括枪击发生的时刻。
加西斯·佩雷斯的移民律师凯特·林肯·戈德芬奇说：“我要求ICE提供行车记录仪录像，我不明白他们为什么不把它交给我们。”。
戴维斯警长表示，奥斯汀警方不知道被解雇的ICE特工是否佩戴了随身摄像头。截至周二的新闻发布会，该部门尚未要求联邦当局提供随身摄像头视频或类似材料。

articles.title_orig: China’s surging biotech sector represents both competition and lifeline for the US
articles.title_zh: China’s surging biotech sector represents both competition and lifeline for the US
articles.content_orig:
As Chinese companies push beyond “me-too” drugs and the country lays out a new five-year plan targeting a $522 billion–strong biotech industry by 2030, experts say more predictable funding and regulation could help the U.S. maintain its edge.
Emerging from stealth earlier this month, Boston-based Solstice Oncology highlighted its origins in a trans-Pacific exchange that’s grown commonplace. The startup licensed its lead asset, colon cancer candidate porustobart, from Chinese biotech Harbour BioMed in February in a deal worth more than $100 million upfront and potentially upwards of $1 billion. Such deals are helping to fuel the rapid growth of Chinese biotech, which is also the beneficiary of decades of focused support by its government.
There’s ample reason to believe that trend will continue: Last week, the Chinese government released a new five-year plan that lays out a goal of $521.8 billion in combined revenue for its domestic biotech industry by 2030. It also aims to originate at least 25% of first-in-class drugs on the global market by that date.
Meanwhile, out-licensing from Chinese biotechs has surged since the start of the COVID-19 pandemic, from 35 such deals worth a total of $989 million in 2019 to 186 deals worth $137.7 billion in 2025, according to data from PharmCube. Evaluate has predicted that Chinese assets will make up more than two-thirds of total deal value this year, up from less than 5% five years ago.
“The number of licensing deals have radically accelerated, wherein large pharmaceutical companies are increasingly turning their business development to China,” Jeremy Levin, executive chairman of Ovid Therapeutics, told BioSpace. “The shift of pharmaceutical licensing activity toward China-originated assets is now an established fact, and two years ago it was far less pronounced.”
Such licensing deals may be a boon to companies like Solstice Oncology, but the rise of Chinese biotech has prompted considerable handwringing about U.S. competitiveness.
“We have to start thinking about what it means if we so erode our innovation base here in the U.S. that we are dependent on a potential adversary for life-sustaining medications,” Caitlin Frazer, executive director of the National Security Commission on Emerging Biotechnology (NSCEB), told BioSpace last month.
The Chinese government’s prioritization of biotech traces back to a 2006 mention of related terms in a medium- and long-term planning document, said Alexander Brown, a senior analyst at the Mercator Institute for China Studies (MERICS). The sector has continued to crop up in government planning documents in the two decades since. While experts say it’s difficult to quantify how much the Chinese government puts into its domestic biotech sector, Brown and a MERICS co-author estimated the investment was at least 20 billion renminbi (about $3 billion) in 2023.
One difficulty in quantifying the government’s support is that it goes beyond direct investment in startups, Cyriac Roeding, CEO of the cancer therapeutics firm Earli, said in an interview. “The Chinese government does a lot of things in many different ways, not just direct investments, but also purchases, like getting into the game as a customer, or cheaper supplies,” he explained.
Levin said the Chinese government’s biotech strategy has taken decades to execute. First, it established the ability to manufacture medications. Next came domestic contract research organizations (CROs). “That gave them the ability to make a molecule and then to test it,” Levin said. “As they did that, they studied very carefully how we approved drugs. And so they established and continually refined their drug approval process in China.”
In step three, China launched clinical trials “in a way that complemented their testing of drugs in the CRO-like environment,” Levin said. “They established a highway which was high speed for the development of so-called lookalikes or bio-betters,” medications based on the mechanism of action of existing drugs developed elsewhere. In step four, the government launched programs aimed at attracting researchers who’d gained valuable training and experience abroad to return and put their skills to work domestically. These programs cover a range of science and engineering fields in addition to biotech.
Some commenters have used the specter of Chinese competition to argue for more streamlined regulation of clinical trials in the U.S. On the flip side of the same coin, two lawmakers called for increased FDA oversight of Chinese study sites and scrutiny of data collected there after several clinical trial deaths in the country. But none of the experts who spoke with BioSpace cited a superior regulatory process as a factor in the rise of the Chinese biotech industry.
“Yes, [regarding the] FDA, there’s a lot of things that can be done better. No question,” Roeding said. But that’s not going to reorient the trajectories of the U.S. and Chinese biotech sectors. Rather, he argued, you have to follow the money.
Roeding pointed out that the billions poured into licensing deals with Chinese companies represent money not going to innovative early-stage research happening stateside. That compounds what he sees as the major factor holding U.S. biotech back as China rises: a lack of consistent funding.
While he conceded that boom and bust cycles have always characterized private investment in U.S. biotech, he said funding for early-stage, innovative research is far worse than in the past because of a prolonged post-COVID bust and because AI ventures are now attracting the vast majority of venture capital investment, leaving little leftover for biotech. And while currently the “XBI looks great,” Roeding said, most investment that does reach biotech goes to clinical-stage companies rather than earlier-stage work.
“This industry is deeply suffering from the lack of consistency. That’s our biggest problem,” Roeding said. “Consistent funding for innovation that has long cycles of time, much longer than others, is critical.”
To accomplish that, he argues for the creation of a publicly funded sovereign wealth fund. Its investments should be concentrated in bust cycles and in bridging the “valley of death” between early, NIH-funded research and clinical validation, he said. “And now you can start flattening the [boom-and-bust investment] curve and you can be internationally competitive.”
Moreover, Roeding added, “the beautiful thing about it is if it’s done right. . . . It’s actually going to pay itself back and more. Society is going to make money off this.”
Levin has a different take. A lack of appreciation for biotech and a failure to differentiate it from pharma mean that the former sector suffers from price-control policies such as the IRA and Most Favored Nation, as well as a health insurance industry that often pushes the cost of drugs onto patients, he said.
Then to add insult to injury, Levin continued, the FDA substantially reduced its workforce last year, laying off about 20% of employees. That loss of institutional knowledge caused what he called “structural damage” that risks widening an already established competitive gap as China moves rapidly in biotechnology.
That said, Chinese biotech faces barriers of its own, Levin noted, especially in their capability to scale, to fully develop drugs on their own and to reach overseas markets. “And that’s why we’re seeing a huge takeoff, also, of out-licensing deals in recent years,” Levin told BioSpace.
“So it’s not all rosy for the Chinese biotech sector,” he continued, “but certainly this long-term government backing and just the fact that they’re able to do research and do certain processes in China at a higher scale, at a cheaper cost, at a faster speed than in other countries is really a core reason why they’re rising so quickly.”

articles.content_orig:
• Trump speech: US President Donald Trump told the UN General Assembly a deal with Iran is possible after the midterm elections, but his other choice is to “annihilate the Islamic Republic.” He also spoke about US munitions stockpiles and plans to establish a “large military presence” on Greenland. When he vowed that Cuba’s communist government “will fall,” the Cuban delegation walked out.
• Iran talks: President Masoud Pezeshkian has landed in New York to attend the General Assembly, Iranian state media reported. Earlier today, the US and Iranian delegations engaged in “lengthy talks” through mediators, US special envoy Steve Witkoff said.
• Meeting with Zelensky: Meanwhile, Trump said he thinks Ukraine and Russia will make a deal but did not give any specifics. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky separately said he is ready for a trilateral meeting with Russia and the US.
Venezuela's acting leader hails first meeting with Trump since Maduro capture
Acting Venezuelan President Delcy Rodríguez hailed her first meeting with US President Donald Trump since the US captured her predecessor Nicolás Maduro as “historic.”
“We discussed strengthening the bilateral relationship between our countries and advancing a cooperation agenda in strategic areas such as energy, mining, and security,” Rodríguez said in a post on X late Tuesday, alongside a photo of the two.
Rodríguez, who spoke to Trump on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, thanked the US President for support during the devastating earthquakes that hit Venezuela in June.
“We will continue to advance a diplomacy that serves the national interest, aimed at achieving concrete results and collective benefits for the Venezuelan people,” she added.
CNN has reached out to the White House for comment on the meeting.
Trump met with Venezuela's acting leader as country carries out US-backed reforms
US President Donald Trump met tonight with acting Venezuelan President Delcy Rodríguez as Washington maintains political pressure on her country to enact reforms.
The meeting, which Rodríguez confirmed on X late Tuesday evening, comes more than eight months after the US captured Rodríguez’s predecessor, strongman leader Nicolás Maduro, in a daring operation in Venezuela.
Maduro is currently being held in a Brooklyn detention center, just miles from the UN General Assembly.
Since Maduro’s capture, the US has compelled Rodríguez’s acting government to open Venezuela’s oil industry to foreign investment, release hundreds of political prisoners, roll back ties with US adversaries such as Cuba, and reestablish diplomatic ties with the US.
Washington says the goal is for Venezuela to eventually transition into a democracy, though Trump has repeatedly said the country isn’t ready for elections yet, and Human Rights Watch says the country still needs institutional reforms to protect people’s basic rights.
During the transition process, the US has largely sidelined Venezuela’s opposition leader Maria Corina Machado, who won the 2025 Nobel Peace Prize for promoting democratic rights in the country.
Some of the global leaders who will be speaking at UNGA this week
The speeches delivered from the United Nations General Assembly podium often attract attention for the behavior of the audience as much as the speakers themselves.
Last year, numerous delegates left the auditorium while Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu spoke. In 2018, laughing delegates interrupted US President Donald Trump’s speech as he outlined his administration’s achievements.
One big question is whether Chinese leader Xi Jinping will make a surprise appearance in New York. Xi is due to appear in Washington for a state visit while the General Assembly is underway.
Other headline speakers include Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who spoke first Tuesday, and Netanyahu, who will speak Thursday, according to a preliminary list.
Venezuelan acting President Delcy Rodríguez will make her UN debut on Wednesday while her former boss, Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, sits in jail mere miles away in Brooklyn.
Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas is slotted for a Thursday speaking time before Netanyahu. However, the Trump administration has again refused Abbas a visa, so he will almost certainly address the chamber via video.
Even as it denies visas to Palestinian officials, the administration will allow Iran’s “core delegation,” which would likely include President Masoud Pezeshkian, to come to New York.
Pezeshkian speaking in New York while his country is actively engaged in combat with the United States is virtually unprecedented. The closest international equivalent might be Egyptian President Anwar Sadat’s 1977 visit to Israel while the two countries were technically at war — but even that was part of a larger peace process.
The role UNGA has played in global events
All eyes are on New York this week as world leaders gather for a high-level meeting of the UN General Assembly, the organization’s main policymaking body, where all its member states are represented. Historically, the assembly has passed some landmark resolutions but its impact has lessened in recent years.
In 1948, member states adopted both the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the Genocide Convention, providing the basis for modern international human rights law. Later, in 1956, the assembly established the first ever UN peacekeeping force during the Suez Canal Crisis to supervise the withdrawal of French, British and Israeli troops from Egypt.
The assembly also approved the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT) in 1968, which aimed to stop more countries developing nuclear weapons. Almost every country joined except Israel, India and Pakistan, while North Korea withdrew from the treaty in 2003, displaying the UN’s limited ability to compel countries to stick to its resolutions. And in 1996, UNGA adopted the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty, helping to almost completely curb the practice.
More recently, however, its resolutions have become less concrete in nature. The assembly endorsed the Responsibility to Protect doctrine in 2005 and established the Human Rights Council in 2006. In 2015 it adopted the Sustainable Development Goals seeking to end poverty, turbocharge climate action and reduce inequality, but progress has been slow in some areas and non-existent in others.

articles.title_orig: Missouri’s embattled, Trump-backed congressional map returns to Supreme Court for a third time
articles.title_zh: Missouri’s embattled, Trump-backed congressional map returns to Supreme Court for a third time
articles.content_orig:
A quixotic legal battle over whether Missouri may use a GOP-friendly congressional redistricting plan for November’s election returned to the Supreme Court for the third time late Tuesday night, forcing the justices to once again review an effort the court unanimously rejected less than two weeks ago.
The emergency appeal will — once again — decide if Republicans can flip an additional House seat in the November midterm election. It’s also part of an extraordinary push by Republicans to continue to fight for the seat after the conservative high court has signaled it is uninterested in getting involved in the messy, months-old dispute over the state’s map.
A group opposed to the map filed the emergency case at the Supreme Court late Tuesday a day after a federal appeals court ruled that Missouri must use the Republican-friendly map in November, rather than a map created in 2022, because voters had already selected nominees based on the newer map in the state’s primary election.
“Ballots using the 2022 map have been printed and mailed, and absentee voting, both by mail and in-person, began today,” the group told the Supreme Court in its appeal. “Those ballots cannot be reassigned to new districts now.”
Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who handles appeals arising from Missouri, requested a response in the case by Wednesday afternoon.
Missouri’s new map targeted the 5th Congressional District, held by Democratic Rep. Emanuel Cleaver, by breaking up its Kansas City base and stretching it into rural and Republican-leaning parts of the state. There would be seven conservative-leaning districts and one Democratic-leaning, a change from the current 6-2 split.
The whipsaw case of Missouri’s congressional map may be merely an appetizer for the banquet of election appeals that are likely to reach the justices tied to this year’s midterms.
The justices have already shut down an effort by President Donald Trump to give the US Postal Service more power to screen mail ballots. The court has also already juggled a series of other redistricting disputes this year, including in Texas, California, Louisiana, Alabama and Virginia.
University of Chicago law professor William Baude said Tuesday that it was “a hundred to one” likely that the court would reject the GOP map again. He described the case as a “taste of what’s to come.”
The Missouri Supreme Court ruled earlier this month that the 7-1 Republican map adopted by the legislature at Trump’s behest last year could not be used because of a referendum challenge brought against it under the state constitution. State Republicans challenged that, appealing all the way up to the US Supreme Court. Kavanaugh, a conservative, declined that request, which appeared to settle the matter.
But minutes after that decision, a federal district court stepped in with a ruling in favor of the GOP map. And the case was once again appealed to the US Supreme Court, which once again sided against reviving the GOP map. In that instance, the full court reviewed the case, and no justices noted their dissent. The court also did not explain its reasoning.
The conservative 8th US Circuit Court of Appeals read the boilerplate language from the Supreme Court, and its lack of reasoning, as an invitation to rush through its own ruling. In an unsigned opinion, the court concluded that “the Constitution does not permit Missouri to use a different congressional district map in the November 2026 general election than it used in the August 2026 primary election.” And it ordered a federal trial court to once again require that the state move forward with the 7-1 map.
It is that decision that has prompted the third round of appeals.
Even though the 8th Circuit ruled in favor of the GOP, it ordered the lower court to pause the impact of that decision until Monday to give the appeals a chance to play out. That means the Supreme Court is likely to either settle the dispute before Monday, or issue a short-term extension of that deadline to give the justices more time to decide.
CNN’s Tierney Sneed contributed to this report.

articles.title_zh: China's Xi kicks off state visit to Washington on Wednesday with a rare planeside welcome from Trump

When Chinese leader Xi Jinping visits Washington this week, he will be sitting down with President Donald Trump in a vastly different position than the last time the two men met face-to-face in the United States nearly a decade ago.
At that 2017 summit at Trump’s Mar-a-Lago resort China was lagging America on multiple fronts and vulnerable to the tech and trade frictions Trump would unleash on it in the coming year.
Now, Xi arrives at the helm of a country that’s transformed.
The world’s second largest economy has emerged as a tech heavyweight. Home-grown tech talent is spurring Chinese AI models ever closer to Silicon Valley’s frontier. Beijing-based space firms are launching and landing reuseable rockets with their sights on global champion SpaceX. Companies from energy to AI, robots and memory chips have launched blockbuster stock debuts over the past year.
China’s manufacturing juggernaut racked up a $1.2 trillion global trade surplus last year, due in part to surging demand for its electric vehicles, solar panels and chips. Its grip on the supply chains for some exports – especially rare earths – has given Beijing unique leverage over Washington and Trump’s “America First” trade war.
And at a moment when the US is antagonizing allies and has yet to find a way to end its war on Iran that’s destabilizing the global economy, Xi has been burnishing China’s image as a responsible and dependable global leader.
Throughout policy circles in Beijing, there is a consensus: gone are the days when the US could make one-directional demands of China.
“China is far more confident than nine years ago and what’s even more important is that today China has found an effective way to keep the US in check,” said Wu Xinbo, dean of the Institute of International Studies at Shanghai’s Fudan University, who advises the government on foreign policy.
“Washington has to treat Beijing with more equality, respect and this relationship has to be more and more reciprocal.”
That doesn’t mean the stakes are low for Xi as he arrives in Washington for an expected three-day stay.
The Chinese leader is banking on China’s high-tech transformation to inject momentum into a slowing economy. Maintaining “constructive strategic stability” – an ambition the two sides agreed to during a meeting in Beijing in May – could help ensure frictions or conflict with the US don’t get in the way.
But buoyed by China’s growing global and technological clout, Xi will also be presenting to the US a new reality: while Beijing wants a stable relationship with the US, its rise doesn’t depend on it.
In a bullish editorial in party mouthpiece the People’s Daily on Wednesday that helps illustrate this confidence, China’s ambassador to the US warned that Taiwan and human rights are “red lines” for Beijing that cannot be crossed.
“China’s sovereignty, security, and development interests must not be violated. The four red lines concerning the Taiwan issue, democracy and human rights, China’s political system and development path, and its right to development must not be challenged,” Xie Feng wrote.
For Xi, a key source of that confidence has been China’s ability to diversify trade away from the US market and build out its technological self-sufficiency – two mandates sharpened by pressures on China from the first Trump administration.
Beijing has funneled vast financing and political will toward building its own technology in cutting-edge sectors – like robotics, AI, biotech, space, new energy and chips – and applying that tech into industry.
The fruits of that growth, however, are not spread evenly. Youth unemployment hit a recent high last month. Hundreds of millions of workers rely on the gig economy, such as delivering food or driving ride-share cars for their primary work. Consumption lags, local governments struggle under debt and a huge property sector crisis rumbles on.
People from all walks of life in China will readily tell you that the economy is just not doing as good as it used to be. But alongside this, there is often a sense of pride that the country has been able to rise as a tech power, even in the face of US-imposed restrictions.
Look no further than the case of Huawei, the Chinese tech giant blacklisted by the first Trump administration. In recent days Chinese tech vloggers have been gleefully posting videos about Apple’s much-hyped release of its first foldable phone. They point out that Huawei’s own foldable model came out seven years ago.
Days ahead of Xi’s visit to the US, Huawei also announced that its next generation of Ascend AI chips would be released ahead of schedule next year, signaling progress in what has been a crucial bottleneck for China in AI development.
“We cannot accept a destiny where we cannot control our fate being determined by others in terms of willingness to sell chips to China or not,” Huawei rotating chairman Eric Xu said earlier this month.
And while the American public is largely pessimistic about the development of AI, their peers in China are more focused on how it might impact their day-to-day lives. Job displacement is a concern, but there’s also a sense there is an opportunity to be seized – and that the ruling Communist Party, with its tight control over society, won’t let the technology spin out of control.
Xi is heading to the US in the middle of an explosion of conversation about the risks of AI, including from Chinese models. Trump has said the country can’t slow development for safety, because it must focus on beating China.
That puts the spotlight on a key aim from Xi and his delegation: to dissuade the US from more tech restrictions that further could limit Chinese firms’ access to American technology or markets.
China wants to see “greater predictability in the economic and technology relationship” and a “stronger political commitment to prevent sensitive issues — especially Taiwan and technology restrictions — from destabilizing the overall relationship,” according to Sun Chenghao, a senior fellow at Tsinghua University’s Center for International Security and Strategy in Beijing.
But this is also where the shifting balance of power between China and the US comes in.
Both sides know that new restrictions – if seen by Beijing as too aggressive – could reignite the conflict that led their economies to the brink of full decoupling last year.
The truce that ended that round of their trade war was reached only after Beijing threatened a massive expansion of export controls on strategically critical rare earths, in response to a US move that would have vastly expanded the number of blacklisted Chinese firms.
That truce will likely be extended this week – and both sides will be wary of pushing the other too far in a situation where “nobody wins, because it’s equally matched,” according to Kurt Tong, managing partner at The Asia Group advisory firm.
“In the economic space, there isn’t really any superior player … because of the equally matched leverage aspects, the two sides are pulling back from actions that cost them to execute,” said Tong, who formerly served as the US consul general of Hong Kong.
Now, Trump “looks at Xi Jinping and sees a counterpart as opposed to someone to wrestle into submission,” he said.
China is now seen more positively than the US in most of 36 countries surveyed in a new Pew Research poll published in July. Xi even edged out Trump in winning people’s confidence, the pollsters found.
These changes come not just alongside a shake-up of the role of the US on the global stage, but a shift in China’s ability to wield soft power. People around the world are using Chinese AI models for their businesses and driving Chinese EVs. Viral cultural exports like the Labubu plushy and Chinese dramas, as well as the online Chinamaxxing trend have driven interest and tourism in China.

And at a moment when the US is antagonizing allies and has yet to find a way to end its war on Iran that’s destabilizing the global economy, Xi has been burnishing China’s image as a responsible and dependable global leader.
Throughout policy circles in Beijing, there is a consensus: gone are the days when the US could make one-directional demands of China.
“China is far more confident than nine years ago and what’s even more important is that today China has found an effective way to keep the US in check,” said Wu Xinbo, dean of the Institute of International Studies at Shanghai’s Fudan University, who advises the government on foreign policy.
“Washington has to treat Beijing with more equality, respect and this relationship has to be more and more reciprocal.”
That doesn’t mean the stakes are low for Xi as he arrives in Washington for an expected three-day stay.
The Chinese leader is banking on China’s high-tech transformation to inject momentum into a slowing economy. Maintaining “constructive strategic stability” – an ambition the two sides agreed to during a meeting in Beijing in May – could help ensure frictions or conflict with the US don’t get in the way.
But buoyed by China’s growing global and technological clout, Xi will also be presenting to the US a new reality: while Beijing wants a stable relationship with the US, its rise doesn’t depend on it.
In a bullish editorial in party mouthpiece the People’s Daily on Wednesday that helps illustrate this confidence, China’s ambassador to the US warned that Taiwan and human rights are “red lines” for Beijing that cannot be crossed.
“China’s sovereignty, security, and development interests must not be violated. The four red lines concerning the Taiwan issue, democracy and human rights, China’s political system and development path, and its right to development must not be challenged,” Xie Feng wrote.
For Xi, a key source of that confidence has been China’s ability to diversify trade away from the US market and build out its technological self-sufficiency – two mandates sharpened by pressures on China from the first Trump administration.
Beijing has funneled vast financing and political will toward building its own technology in cutting-edge sectors – like robotics, AI, biotech, space, new energy and chips – and applying that tech into industry.
The fruits of that growth, however, are not spread evenly. Youth unemployment hit a recent high last month. Hundreds of millions of workers rely on the gig economy, such as delivering food or driving ride-share cars for their primary work. Consumption lags, local governments struggle under debt and a huge property sector crisis rumbles on.
People from all walks of life in China will readily tell you that the economy is just not doing as good as it used to be. But alongside this, there is often a sense of pride that the country has been able to rise as a tech power, even in the face of US-imposed restrictions.
Look no further than the case of Huawei, the Chinese tech giant blacklisted by the first Trump administration. In recent days Chinese tech vloggers have been gleefully posting videos about Apple’s much-hyped release of its first foldable phone. They point out that Huawei’s own foldable model came out seven years ago.
Days ahead of Xi’s visit to the US, Huawei also announced that its next generation of Ascend AI chips would be released ahead of schedule next year, signaling progress in what has been a crucial bottleneck for China in AI development.
“We cannot accept a destiny where we cannot control our fate being determined by others in terms of willingness to sell chips to China or not,” Huawei rotating chairman Eric Xu said earlier this month.
And while the American public is largely pessimistic about the development of AI, their peers in China are more focused on how it might impact their day-to-day lives. Job displacement is a concern, but there’s also a sense there is an opportunity to be seized – and that the ruling Communist Party, with its tight control over society, won’t let the technology spin out of control.
Xi is heading to the US in the middle of an explosion of conversation about the risks of AI, including from Chinese models. Trump has said the country can’t slow development for safety, because it must focus on beating China.
That puts the spotlight on a key aim from Xi and his delegation: to dissuade the US from more tech restrictions that further could limit Chinese firms’ access to American technology or markets.
China wants to see “greater predictability in the economic and technology relationship” and a “stronger political commitment to prevent sensitive issues — especially Taiwan and technology restrictions — from destabilizing the overall relationship,” according to Sun Chenghao, a senior fellow at Tsinghua University’s Center for International Security and Strategy in Beijing.
But this is also where the shifting balance of power between China and the US comes in.
Both sides know that new restrictions – if seen by Beijing as too aggressive – could reignite the conflict that led their economies to the brink of full decoupling last year.
The truce that ended that round of their trade war was reached only after Beijing threatened a massive expansion of export controls on strategically critical rare earths, in response to a US move that would have vastly expanded the number of blacklisted Chinese firms.
That truce will likely be extended this week – and both sides will be wary of pushing the other too far in a situation where “nobody wins, because it’s equally matched,” according to Kurt Tong, managing partner at The Asia Group advisory firm.
“In the economic space, there isn’t really any superior player … because of the equally matched leverage aspects, the two sides are pulling back from actions that cost them to execute,” said Tong, who formerly served as the US consul general of Hong Kong.
Now, Trump “looks at Xi Jinping and sees a counterpart as opposed to someone to wrestle into submission,” he said.
China is now seen more positively than the US in most of 36 countries surveyed in a new Pew Research poll published in July. Xi even edged out Trump in winning people’s confidence, the pollsters found.
These changes come not just alongside a shake-up of the role of the US on the global stage, but a shift in China’s ability to wield soft power. People around the world are using Chinese AI models for their businesses and driving Chinese EVs. Viral cultural exports like the Labubu plushy and Chinese dramas, as well as the online Chinamaxxing trend have driven interest and tourism in China.

articles.title_orig: Worries about an AI internet takeover gain new urgency among doomsday scenarios
articles.title_zh: Worries about an AI internet takeover gain new urgency among doomsday scenarios
articles.content_orig:
I visited the CEO of a major startup in SF last week. He recounted a tale that blew my mind.
His company recently put a new product online but hadn't done a big launch or any marketing. Within a week or two, it got at least a million signups. Barely any humans even knew about it. This was all AI agents just finding this new tool and using it en masse.
This is the future of the internet, and it's arriving at warp speed.
Back in early 2025, I described a vision of a "dark internet" where humans will be drowned out by agents accessing and using online information, widgets, and tools all by themselves.
Silicon Valley got busy building the "rails" for this agentic web so that these autonomous software programs could act on our behalf, executing workflows, doing online chores, and even paying for things, all without us lifting a finger.
This took a couple of years, but the early foundations have been built and that's been enough to support a sudden surge in agent activity online, producing both stunning and worrying results.
Meta recently launched a personal agent called Muse, which got busy scouring the web and calling customer service on behalf of millions of users. It hit the top of the app charts late Thursday. Instinct, an agent that lives in your text messages, is performing similar feats.
In the workplace, coding agents are churning out millions of lines of code faster than any human software engineer. And some of these bots have broken out of online testing environments, sparking new predictions of AI doom and calls for an industry slowdown.
That's unlikely to stop the agentic internet from exploding and changing how our lives and businesses are run in unprecedented ways.
Bot traffic overtook human traffic online a few months ago, and it could become 1,000 times bigger than human-generated traffic in about five years, according to Cloudflare estimates.
"Humans will be a rounding error on the internet, not because human traffic goes down, but that's just how fast we're seeing non-human traffic grow," Cloudflare CFO Thomas Seifert said earlier this year.
"AI agentic Internet traffic will obviously VASTLY exceed human usage. Not a close call at all," Elon Musk wrote on X following the Cloudflare projection.
An internet designed for machines is likely to be very different from the one that was built over the past few decades for humans.
Take a look at this video posted this week on X by Gregor Žunič, cofounder of Browser Use, a startup that's developing an AI agent framework for controlling web browsers and automating online tasks.
It shows an agent using Google to find the best flight from Zurich to London on a specific date. It took the bot seven seconds, way faster than a human could do it.
Breaking: Browser Use + Jev = Ultrafast ⚡
Findings flights took 7s and cost only $0.0039 🤯
> new action space every step
> small LLM fallback to type
(this video is at 1x speed btw)
Built a tiny open source browser agent. try it below ↓ pic.twitter.com/AplCBRYC5o
Imagine this happening millions of times a second on sites built for human, not machine, speed?
As with all powerful new technology, the agentic internet will produce good and bad outcomes. And we're already seeing both.
Since Meta's Muse launched last week, early users have been recounting stories of the agent going out on the web to find and negotiate new subscriptions, insurance policies, and other cost savings.
Joseph Devoy, founder of startup Tempo, posted on X that he saved thousands of dollars by uploading his auto insurance policy to Muse and asking the agent to find a better rate with identical coverage. It took five minutes to find a cheaper option, according to Devoy.
Yesterday I uploaded my auto insurance policy to Meta @Muse and asked for a better rate with identical coverage. In ~5 minutes, it found a policy saving me $3,500 /year, bought it, and canceled my old one.
I knew I was overpaying. I’d abandoned several attempts to switch because… pic.twitter.com/HlIweoWN2K
Too much tech hype? Then trust my colleague Pranav Dixit who put Instinct through its paces recently. In just a few days, it booked travel, ordered groceries, dealt with customer service, canceled subscriptions, answered emails, and even faxed paperwork to his bank. He was impressed.
Other users say Muse negotiated a lower internet bill, found forgotten subscriptions, and even spotted an Adobe payment that had somehow been tied to someone else's account.
The stories come with caveats. Some users have posted examples of Muse inventing information during phone calls or making mistakes that humans had to fix.
There are more worrying developments. OpenAI and Anthropic have reported several incidents recently where their AI models and agents escaped testing environments and hacked into servers and websites, with the Hugging Face episode getting the most attention.
This has sparked another round of AI doomer pronouncements and a broader debate about AI safety and alignment. Indeed, making sure agents do what you tell them in a responsible way will be a key challenge in this new era of the internet.
Even when agents work well, there will be challenges as the online world adjusts to this new digital reality. Actually, if agents work really, really well, the problems could be bigger.
Take the example of Tempo's Devoy and how he used Meta's Muse agent to save a lot of money on insurance.
"Insurance companies (and banks) should be TERRIFIED," Angela Strange, a general partner at VC firm Andreessen Horowitz, wrote on X. "Muse found a new/cheaper policy, and canceled the old one. Inertia and information asymmetry will no longer be enough to keep customers."
More recently, when my colleague Pranav had Muse call his insurance company, he said the company declined to talk to the bot because their policy doesn't allow them to talk to unauthorized AI agents.
You can bet any company getting bombarded by deal-seeking AI agents will be frantically readying similar responses, so they don't lose out on millions of dollars.
Even when it's not purely about money, some agent activity is getting cut off after being too persistent. A VC recently tried using Instinct to book him a table at a fancy New York restaurant. The agent bombarded American Express's Resy booking service so much that the platform temporarily shut down his account.
"Resy does not currently permit unapproved third-party bots or agents to independently access or interact with the Resy platform," an American Express spokesperson told Business Insider. "Unapproved automated activity can introduce risks to the platform and compromise a fair reservation experience for diners."
Agent access will be a fascinating fight as the internet molds to the march of the machines. It's not as simple as blocking these bots, though. If enough human users sign up for new agentic services and tools, businesses may have no choice but to do business with bots.
For instance, Amazon blocks ChatGPT bots online, but that risks missing out on opportunities to sell to OpenAI's 1 billion monthly human users. The two companies recently announced an advertising partnership that hints at more coordination going forward.
This, I think, is where the agentic internet is headed. If these tools are useful enough, companies will have to adapt and engage with the machines.

articles.title_orig: Defending reporter ban, Justice Department argues stories on Trump’s ballroom project, Iran war threaten national security
articles.title_zh: Defending reporter ban, Justice Department argues stories on Trump’s ballroom project, Iran war threaten national security
articles.content_orig:
The Justice Department said late Tuesday that CNN, MS NOW and Politico can be shut out from areas of the White House at the president’s will. The lawyers argue that the outlets’ coverage of the Iran war and of President Donald Tump’s ballroom construction could amount to a national security risk that justifies the ban.
A court filing from the Trump administration late Tuesday night argues “access to the White House is a privilege, not a right,” in spite of First Amendment protections around press freedom.
The filing also argues Trump can control private areas of the White House to protect national security information that may be inside the complex – an argument in line with other abrupt lockdowns and changes Trump has made to the White House.
“At the very least, the Government may control reporters’ access to restricted presidential areas, such as the Oval Office, even for viewpoint-discriminatory reasons,” the Justice Department wrote to the court.
“The President has found that Plaintiffs have engaged in a number of reporting incidents that have threatened national security. Such reporting directly raises national security concerns.”
The filings came on the eve of an emergency hearing before federal judge Timothy Kelly in Washington, DC. CNN, MS NOW and Politico are asking for the court to immediately restore their access to the White House.
The case is a critical test of First Amendment protections and has prompted suspensions of live coverage of Trump by the major TV networks, National Public Radio and still photographers in the White House press corps.
While the Justice Department is arguing for the president’s prerogatives, the federal court in Washington, DC, has repeatedly restored journalists’ press access at the White House when administrations have tried to take it away. That includes by setting the law in the nation’s capital in favor of press freedoms and due process protections for news outlets.
New letters to outlets citing stories about East Wing ballroom, Iran war
The new court filings include letters to the three outlets, dated Tuesday, explaining the president’s cited reasons for the ban. A key claim the media companies have made in the case is that the White House violated their due process rights by failing to give them any written warning before cutting off their access and by depriving the journalists the opportunity to contest the ban. The DOJ pointed to the letters to argue that the due process claims should fail.
The letters cite various stories published by the news organizations and give the reporters until Friday to offer written submissions objecting to the bans.
The letter to CNN cites its reporting on Trump’s plans to build a “top secret” bunker below the East Wing ballroom he is constructing, as well as several stories by the network about the Iran war.
It said CNN had failed to uphold the “expectations” of White House press badge holders because of “reporting incidents” that “threatened national security and/or spread falsehoods.”
The letter to MS NOW, meanwhile, criticizes its coverage of the war in Iran and a story about a leak probe, while Politico was targeted because of stories related to the Iran, the ballroom and Russia sanctions discussions.
